# Part 8: Operations and Measurement

## 8.1 Production readiness as a gate with teeth

**A gate nobody can fail is not a gate.** The test of a readiness process is simple and uncomfortable: how many systems has it stopped. If the answer is none, the gate is a form and the organization is shipping on optimism with a signature attached.

Readiness has **eight dimensions**. Each has a small number of binary conditions, each condition has an evidence artifact rather than an assertion and each dimension has a named signatory who is accountable for the answer.

| Dimension | Conditions that must be satisfied | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Functional** | Scope stated with explicit exclusions; behavior on out-of-scope input defined; output contract enforced outside the model | Scope statement, contract schema, refusal behavior test |
| **Evaluation** | Eval suite exists; baseline recorded; performance known **by segment**; retrieval measured separately where present; thresholds agreed with the business owner | Eval report with segment breakdown |
| **Resilience** | Behavior defined for four failure classes: transient, validation, business-rule and permission; timeouts and retry policy set; degraded mode defined; load tested at peak and at three times peak | Failure matrix, load test results |
| **Security** | Tool capability reviewed against role need; authorization enforced outside the model; injection tested against retrieved and tool content; secrets and egress reviewed | Threat review, penetration test note |
| **Governance** | Data path documented; retention and deletion designed including derived artifacts; approvals recorded; risk assessment complete; user-facing disclosure agreed | Data flow, records schedule, approval log |
| **Operational** | Named operational owner who is not the architect; runbook; on-call route; observability sufficient to answer "what happened on request X" without redeploying; rollback without a deployment | Runbook, ownership record, trace demo |
| **Commercial** | Cost per completed outcome known at expected and at three times expected volume; budget approved; unit economics clear the business case | Sizing model, budget approval |
| **Change** | Prompt, model, tool, corpus and guardrail changes all trigger an eval run; versioning in place; no path to production that bypasses the gate | Change policy, pipeline configuration |

**Two design rules make the gate real.** **Every condition is binary and evidenced**: "security reviewed" is not a condition, "threat review completed and findings closed or accepted in writing" is. And **failing a condition produces one of exactly three outcomes**: remediate and re-present, ship with a time-bounded accepted risk signed by a named person, or do not ship. The absence of a fourth outcome is what gives the gate teeth.

**Two questions the eight dimensions do not ask on their own face, and both belong in the evidence.** The first is human review: is there a routing rule, a reviewer capacity assumption and a handoff package. A quality threshold implies a destination for everything that misses it and the capacity to absorb it, and neither is visible in a functional scope statement. The second is documentation: could a competent person who has never met you operate, diagnose and change this system. That is a stricter test than the presence of a runbook, and it is set out under documentation and handoff below.

### Who signs, and what they are signing

| Signatory | Dimension | What they are actually accepting |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Business owner** | Functional, evaluation, commercial | That the measured quality is good enough for their process, and that they own the residual error rate |
| **Operational owner** | Resilience, operational | That their team can run, diagnose and roll this back at 3am |
| **Security owner** | Security | That the capability granted matches the role and that authorization does not depend on the model |
| **Governance, risk management and compliance owner** | Governance | That the data path, retention and disclosure position are defensible to a regulator |
| **Engineering owner** | Change | That nothing reaches production without an eval run |

**The business owner's signature is the one people misunderstand.** They are not signing that the system is accurate. They are signing that they accept a known error rate on a named population with a defined routing rule for the remainder. That framing turns the conversation from reassurance into risk acceptance, which is the conversation you want on the record.

**When several conditions are unanswered at once, the absence that matters most is measurement or ownership**, because those two are the ones whose absence prevents you from ever fixing the others. Most of what the gate asks for is something a prototype legitimately does not have, and the transition to production is precisely the work of acquiring it.

**Decision rule:** if no condition in the gate could plausibly have blocked any system your organization shipped last year, the gate is decorative and should be rebuilt around binary evidenced conditions.

### ⌂ The architect's lens

**The enterprise question this section does not ask.** A gate with no approver column is a checklist. Who prepares the evidence for each row, who accepts it, what happens when a row is amber rather than green and who owns the thing once it is through.

**Governance at this decision.**

| Decision here | Governance decision that belongs with it | Artifact and owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Answering each readiness question | A named preparer and a named approver per row | Readiness board with owner and approver columns. Steering committee |
| Deciding to go live | Quorum, a recorded decision and a pass-with-conditions option carrying a date | Signed go or no-go record. Steering committee |
| Declaring a system production ready | A named service owner who is not on the delivery team | Service catalog entry with a support model. Service owner |
| Moving from demonstration to service | A funded run budget and a cost center from year one onward | Approved run budget line. Finance business partner |
| Replacing a manual step | Retiring the control that step performed, or re-performing it elsewhere | **The control mapping is a section of the decommissioning plan specified in 10.6, and the plan has one owner, the service owner.** It sits against that plan's manual capability restoration workstream. The process owner is accountable for the control being retired and is consulted on the section, not on the plan |
| Embedding the system in a business process | What the process does when the system is unavailable or degraded | Continuity position and manual fallback procedure. Process owner |

**What this costs the organization.** Launching first and deciding retention later creates a population of regulated records with no defined retention period, which is a finding rather than a backlog item. Most production systems are abandoned not because they failed but because nobody was funded to keep them. **A line nobody can sign is an obligation nobody owns**, and in most organizations the two unsignable lines are the fully loaded cost and the evidence that would be shown to a regulator. Two costs are routinely forgotten. Change management is the first: training, communication and redesigning the surrounding process are where most enterprise deployments fail and none of them appears on a technical gate. The manual fallback is the second: a process that has lost the ability to run without the assistant has acquired a single point of failure it did not previously have, and rebuilding that capability later is expensive.

**The executive translation.** This is a stage gate with named approvers and three outcomes, pass with conditions and a date is usually the right answer rather than a delay, and the distance between a demonstration and a service is an owner, a budget and a plan for the day it is down.

### Where a proof of concept misleads

The gate above assumes something has been built. **The distance between the thing that was demonstrated and the thing that has to pass the gate is where most readiness work actually lives**, and it is predictable enough to be named in advance.

A proof of concept is designed to demonstrate capability. It runs at low volume, on clean inputs, with a patient user. A production system runs at the volume the business generates, on real inputs, in front of users with no tolerance for a slow or incorrect response. **Four dimensions carry almost all of the difference, and a demo conceals all four by construction.**

| Dimension | Why it is invisible in a demo | What it looks like when it fails |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Cost** | Ten to fifty requests a day produces a negligible bill. Monthly cost at production volume is a different calculation entirely | The billing figure exceeds the budget signed off at project approval, and the architecture is renegotiated after deployment |
| **Latency** | A demo runs one request at a time. The p95 under concurrent load is a different number from the median under a single request | Service level breaches and user abandonment. Latency acceptable in a demo can be unacceptable in a real-time workflow |
| **Reliability** | A demo has no retry logic, no fallback and no circuit breaker. When it fails the developer refreshes. There are no users waiting | Any transient failure takes the whole user-facing workflow down instead of degrading gracefully |
| **Failure modes** | A demo is tested on the inputs the developer expected. Production supplies the ones nobody thought of, and the modes are specific to the architecture | Silent degradation, fabricated outputs on edge-case inputs, or complete failure on an input class that was never tested |

**The compact statement of all four rows: a proof of concept establishes capability and establishes nothing else.** It is not a cost model, not a distribution model and not a reliability model, and the failure that follows is almost always a proof of concept quietly promoted into all three at once. Where demonstration figures are shown to a business owner, extrapolate them to expected volume with the error bounds stated, because raw demonstration costs presented without that step become the number the budget was approved against.

**The demo also gives the first signal on whether the system moves the business metric, and that signal is worth capturing deliberately.** Measure the outcome the business owner cares about on the sample, before modeling production cost. A cost profile that fits the budget on a system that produces no measurable improvement in the metric that matters is still a failed deployment.

### What breaks first, by architecture

The fourth dimension deserves its own table, because "test the edge cases" is not actionable and the failure that arrives first is a function of the shape you chose.

| Architecture | What breaks first | Mitigation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Agent** | Unbounded tool use and growing context. An agent that can call tools without budget constraints or turn limits runs up cost and latency in ways that stay invisible until a single request exceeds the ceiling | Per-turn token budgets, maximum tool call counts and explicit stopping criteria. Constrain the tool set to the minimum required. Evaluate the stopping behavior, not only the output quality |
| **Retrieval-augmented generation** | Retrieval quality drift. The retrieval layer degrades when documents are added or removed without reindexing, when the query and the document representation fall out of alignment, or when the index refresh schedule creates staleness for live-state queries | Keep retrieval quality inside the evaluation loop. Monitor retrieval precision and recall as system metrics rather than only output quality. Separate live-state queries from static knowledge queries |
| **Document processing pipeline** | No exception path for low-confidence extractions. A pipeline routing every document through the same flow regardless of extraction confidence produces wrong outputs on edge cases at the same rate it produces correct ones on clean documents | Confidence scoring at the extraction step. Route low-confidence extractions to a human review queue rather than to downstream processing. Include edge cases and difficult documents in the evaluation set |
| **Orchestrator and workers** | Failure boundaries between the orchestrator and its subagents blur, traces fragment and a dropped subagent fails silently at synthesis | Define recoverable failures, which belong to the subagent as a retry or a flag, against unrecoverable ones, which belong to the orchestrator. A shared trace identifier across all agents. Reconcile coverage at synthesis so results equal units submitted |

**The pattern across all four rows: the failure is a consequence of the shape, not of the prompt.** An architecture chosen in 2.4 arrives with its characteristic first failure attached, and naming it during design is cheaper than discovering it during the readiness review.


## 8.2 Evaluation: criteria, datasets and graders

Prompts and artificial intelligence systems are chronically under-tested because they look like they work. The output is fluent, so it looks fine, and fluency is not accuracy. Three paths present themselves after writing a prompt and two of them are traps: ship it after one try, or test against a handful of hand-picked inputs and tweak until they pass. Both feel like testing and prove almost nothing. The third is an evaluation pipeline that scores performance across many cases and produces a number.

**The value of the number is not its level; it is that comparison becomes possible.** Without it, "better" means "I like it more now." It is also what makes the standing instruction operable: add complexity only when it **demonstrably** improves outcomes, and demonstrably requires a number.

**You cannot improve what you have not defined.** An eyeball check across three examples proves nothing. The evaluation suite is the durable asset here, not the prompt: prompts get rewritten constantly, and the dataset and the graders are what let anyone rewrite them safely.

### The suite comes before the production code

The argument above is for having evaluations. This is the separate and more contested claim about **when**, and it is the one that changes how a project runs. **The eval suite is written before the production code, not after it as a quality assurance step.** The default order is to build, look at the output, decide it seems right and test later, and that order forfeits three things that only exist while the code is still unwritten.

| What writing the suite first forces | Why it is unavailable later |
| --- | --- |
| **Stating what success means in measurable terms** | After the build, the measurable definition tends to be reverse-engineered from what the system already does, which is the same defect as setting an eval threshold after seeing the result |
| **Exposing design assumptions while changing them is still cheap** | An assumption discovered at the whiteboard costs an afternoon. The same assumption discovered against working code costs the code |
| **Owning a gate that can adjudicate any later change** | A gate built after the fact has no pre-change baseline, so the first thing it can measure is the second change, not the first |

**The test that decides whether a behavior is buildable as specified: if you cannot write an eval for a behavior, you have no way to measure whether it is present.** That is not a documentation gap. It means every subsequent change to the system is unverifiable with respect to that behavior, so the behavior is being maintained on assertion. A specification containing behaviors nobody can write an eval for has not been fully specified, and naming them at design time is cheaper than discovering them at handover.

**The threshold comes from the business requirement, not from the prototype.** Where the requirement is total accuracy on structured fields, a bounded fabrication rate and schema compliance at a stated percentage, those are the numbers. What the first prototype happens to achieve is an observation, and adopting it as the threshold converts a requirement into a description of current behavior.

#### The workflow, and what each stage hands to the next

The suite is built in five stages and each produces an artifact the next stage consumes. Stating them as artifacts rather than activities is what makes the sequence auditable.

| Stage | What happens | Artifact produced |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1. Define the task** | State the behavior under evaluation in specific measurable terms and write the prompt that will test it. A vague definition produces a vague eval, and the concreteness of both the specification and the prompt is what makes the score mean anything | Task specification with the test prompt and the pass criteria |
| **2. Build the golden dataset** | Assemble the inputs the system will actually meet, including edge cases and counterexamples. **If the dataset is not representative, the scores are not meaningful**, whatever their level | Labeled dataset with expected outputs |
| **3. Run automated checks** | Pass each case through the system and compare against the expected result. Reserve this stage for the unambiguous: format compliance, schema validation, lookups against authoritative data | Pass or fail record per item |
| **4. Score with a judge** | For behavior needing interpretation, tone, reasoning soundness, edge-case appropriateness, a model grader scores at scale against a rubric | Score per item with reasoning |
| **5. Interpret and act** | Aggregate to locate the system and to say whether a change moved it. **A change raising the mean while degrading edge cases or adversarial inputs has not improved the system** | Overall score with a per-category breakdown |

**Adversarial and degraded inputs belong in stage 2, not in a later hardening pass.** Documents with missing fields, handwritten sections, unusual formatting and non-standard layouts are the population the system will meet. A golden dataset built only from clean inputs produces scores that do not predict production, and it produces them confidently.

#### The stale suite, which is worse than no suite

**The highest-risk moment for an undetected regression is not the absence of evals. It is the presence of evals that are out of date.** A suite whose golden dataset predates a prompt revision keeps passing, because it is scoring the behavior the old prompt produced. The scores look stable precisely because nothing in the set is testing what changed. The team reads a green board and ships.

This is the failure mode behind the most common eval postmortem. A suite is built early from the handful of inputs the team had during development, which are convenient rather than representative. The prompt is later revised and the dataset is not. Two weeks after deployment the system is found failing on a class of inputs it was never tested against, and the eval suite that would have caught it had been passing throughout. Both defects, an unrepresentative dataset and a dataset that was not kept current, are invisible until production exposes them.

Two rules follow. **The eval set is updated in the same change as the behavior it measures**, which makes it part of the change rather than a downstream chore. And **manual spot-checks are not an eval substitute**: a spot-check confirms that a chosen input produces a chosen output, and says nothing about behavior on the inputs nobody chose.

### Four tests for a success criterion

The four tests, and the examples in the bad and good columns, follow Anthropic's success-criteria documentation.

| Test | Meaning | Bad | Good |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Specific** | Define what you want to achieve | "Good performance" | "Accurate sentiment classification" |
| **Measurable** | Quantitative metrics, or well-defined qualitative scales consistently applied | "Safe outputs" | "Fewer than 0.1% of outputs across 10,000 trials flagged for toxicity by our content filter" |
| **Achievable** | Base targets on industry benchmarks, prior experiments, research or expert knowledge | A target beyond current frontier capability | A target grounded in a measured baseline |
| **Relevant** | Align to the application's purpose | Citation accuracy for a casual chatbot | Citation accuracy for a medical application |

The safety row is worth studying because it carries the point that generalizes: **even hazy topics such as ethics and safety can be quantified.** An unmeasurable commitment is converted into a rate over a population, measured by a named instrument.

### The eight common criteria

Task fidelity; consistency; relevance and coherence; tone and style; privacy preservation; context utilization; latency; price.

Two observations. **Privacy preservation and context utilization are evaluation criteria**, not only design properties, which means they are things you measure rather than assert. And **most use cases need multidimensional evaluation along several criteria**, so a single metric offered as sufficient is almost always insufficient.

### The five metric families

**Accuracy**, task-appropriate:

| Task | Measure |
| --- | --- |
| Extraction | Field-level correctness, and separately whether absent information was correctly reported absent rather than fabricated |
| Classification | Correct rate **by class**, because overall accuracy hides total failure on a rare class |
| Question answering over documents | Whether the answer is correct **and** whether the cited source supports it. Two different failures |
| Generation | Rubric score against defined criteria |
| Agentic work | Task completion rate, plus how often the system took an action it should not have |

**Latency.** Time-to-first-token and total time, as distributions.

**Cost.** Per request, and more usefully **per completed outcome**.

**Safety.** Two-sided: harmful-output rate, and **false refusal rate**. Refusing a valid request is a failure in its own right and belongs in the measurement, not only in the guardrail design.

**Security.** Resistance to injected instructions in retrieved or tool content; absence of leakage across users or tenants; refusal of attempts to reach unauthorized capability.

**Two rules.** Pair every quality metric with a cost or latency metric, or you will optimize one into the other and call it progress. And define the metric before making the change.

### Dataset composition and hygiene

Representative cases matching the real distribution; **edge cases chosen deliberately**, being ambiguous, malformed, empty, adversarial, unusually long and cases where information is genuinely absent; and regression cases from real failures, added permanently once fixed.

Freeze the set once it exists. Add to it, but do not quietly edit it, or comparisons across versions stop meaning anything.

### How many cases, and the set that stops working

Two questions about the evaluation set are asked late and should be asked first.

**How many cases.** The honest answer is that it depends on the effect you need to detect and how noisy the measure is, and the useful answer is a floor and a method. The floor is thirty to fifty cases per segment you intend to report on, not thirty to fifty in total, because a set that cannot be broken out by segment will report an aggregate that conceals the regression you care about. The method is to work backwards from the decision: if the decision is "ship if accuracy does not drop", then the set must be large enough that a drop worth caring about is distinguishable from run-to-run variation. Measure the variation before sizing the set. Run the unchanged system against the set several times, look at the spread and treat that spread as the noise floor: a difference smaller than the noise floor is not a result, whatever the mean says. A set of forty cases on a task with a five-point spread cannot detect a three-point improvement, and no amount of confidence in the change will make it able to.

**The set that stops working.** An evaluation set iterated against for six months has quietly become a training set. Every prompt revision was selected because it moved the score on those specific cases, so the score now measures fit to the set rather than capability on the task, and the gap shows up as a system that evaluates well and disappoints in production. Two habits prevent it. Hold out a portion of the set from the start, never look at it during iteration and check it only at a release gate, accepting that a hold-out consulted twice is no longer held out. And rotate: retire cases that every version has passed for several cycles, since they discriminate nothing, and replace them from production failures, which is the only source of cases the design did not anticipate.

⧉ **The tell that a set has stopped working is a rising score with a flat or falling production metric.** When the harness and the field disagree, the field is right and the harness is the thing under investigation. Treat the divergence as a defect in the evaluation, look first at whether the set still resembles the live distribution and resist the reading that production is noisy. Production is the population; the set is the sample.

**A third failure sits between the two above and is the most common of the three: the suite that is present, is run on every change and is misconfigured in a way nothing surfaces.** It fails in two ways and they compound. The dataset is drawn from the inputs that were convenient during development rather than from the live distribution, so it measures a different system from the one shipped. And the expected outputs are not revised when the prompt is, so the suite goes on scoring the behavior the prompt no longer produces and passes for exactly that reason. **A score that does not move across several substantive changes is not stable, it is disconnected**, and the stability that reads as reassurance is the symptom.

The corollary is worth stating because it is resisted. **Manual spot-checks are not a small evaluation suite; they are a different instrument answering a smaller question.** A spot-check confirms that a known input produces an acceptable output. It says nothing about unknown inputs, which is the entire population the system will meet, and a team that has spot-checked ten cases has tested the ten cases it already had opinions about.

### Evaluating a multi-step system

The metric families table gives agentic work one line, correct and insufficient. Task completion is a property of the final step, and everything worth knowing about a multi-step system happened before it.

**Outcome and trajectory answer different questions and neither substitutes for the other.**

| | Outcome evaluation | Trajectory evaluation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Asks** | Did the run end in the correct state | Was the route one you would approve |
| **Instrument** | Final answer or system state against an expected value | The step sequence, checked against constraints |
| **Blind to** | The over-broad query, the write attempted before the entitlement check, the retry masking a permission failure, the answer taken from a stale cache | Legitimate variation. A shorter route to the same state scores as a deviation |
| **Insufficient alone when** | The run changes state, or the route carries the governance property | More than one valid route exists, normal above the fifth rung |

Weighting the two into a composite discards both. **Score the outcome as the primary metric and score the trajectory against constraints rather than against a reference path**: no tool outside the allowlist, no state-changing call before the check authorizing it, no call repeated identically, no more calls than agreed. That converts trajectory evaluation from "did it follow the path we imagined" into "did it stay inside the envelope", which is checkable in code and does not penalize a better route.

**Partial credit is necessary and it is where a multi-step metric usually goes wrong.** A binary pass on a nine-step task discards the information that eight steps worked, and binary failures cannot distinguish a system dying at step one from one dying at step eight: different defects with different owners. The wrong construction is a fraction of steps completed, because it rewards activity: an agent taking twelve steps to fail scores above one failing in three. **Score the step whose failure caused the run to fail, not every step the run performed.** Per failed run, record the first step whose output was wrong and report the distribution of first-failing steps. Where a numeric score is needed, fix the checkpoints in advance as required intermediate states, so the denominator comes from the task rather than the run.

**Attribution across steps depends on replay, not on inference.** In a multi-step run the visible failure is downstream of the causal one, and the final output shows only where damage surfaced. The instrument is a run reconstructible step by step from the log, which is what the tool call records in 4.8 exist for: calls with arguments and results, in order, on one correlation identifier. The analysis is then mechanical: walk forward to the first step whose output was wrong given its input, and that step owns the failure. The qualifier is load-bearing, since a step producing a wrong answer from a wrong input did not fail; its predecessor did, and charging it sends the fix to the wrong component.

**Tool call correctness is its own measure, with three failures sharing nothing but their symptom.**

| Failure | What it is | First remedy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Wrong tool selected** | Right intent, wrong instrument. Concentrates where descriptions overlap or catalogs are large | Descriptions and boundaries; deferred definitions from roughly ten tools per 8.10 |
| **Right tool, wrong arguments** | A well-formed call asking the wrong question: wrong identifier, wrong date range, an over-broad filter | Tighter schemas, enumerations rather than free text and validation that rejects rather than coerces |
| **Right call, result misread** | The tool returned the correct result and the model drew the wrong conclusion | Result shape: fewer fields, explicit units and an explicit empty result rather than an empty list |

All three surface as one completion failure, and a single tool error rate merges three defects with three owners.

**Stopping and cost separate a passing system from an operable one.** An agent completing the task in forty tool calls where five would do passes the completion metric and fails the operating one. Report calls per run, wall clock, tokens and fully loaded cost as distributions, and evaluate stopping in both directions: the run that will not stop and is killed by the per-request bound in 8.10, arriving as a completion failure, and the run that stops early and calls a partial result finished, arriving as a quality failure. Both are stopping failures.

**A worked illustration.** Sixty cases against a supplier-query agent with four tools.

| Measure | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Outcome correct | 46 of 60, 76.7 percent |
| Outcome correct **and** trajectory inside the envelope | 41 of 60, 68.3 percent |
| Correct by an unapproved route | 5, all of them a write attempted before the entitlement check |
| First-failing step, of the 14 failures | 9 retrieval, 3 tool argument construction, 2 final synthesis |
| Tool calls per completed run | p50 6, p95 22 |
| Runs killed by the call bound | 3, counted once as outcome failures and once as stopping failures |

The headline number is 76.7 percent. The number governing whether this system may act unsupervised is 68.3 percent, and the gap between them is why both measures exist. The first-failing-step distribution sends nine of the fourteen failures to the retrieval owner, where an outcome-only report would have sent all fourteen to the prompt. And a p95 of twenty-two calls against a p50 of six is a cost problem invisible in every quality figure above it.

### Multi-turn evaluation, which is a different category again

Multi-step and multi-turn are routinely treated as one thing and they are not. **A multi-step evaluation scores one task executed across several internal steps. A multi-turn evaluation scores a conversation across several exchanges with a user.** The section above governs the first. This governs the second, and a system passing every single-turn case can still fail its users on the third exchange.

**A single-turn eval set cannot tell you how the system holds up across a conversation**, because the unit it scores is one prompt and one response. Three properties only become observable once the unit is a whole conversation.

| What multi-turn evaluation checks | The failure it catches |
| --- | --- |
| **Whether prior context is kept straight across turns** | The system contradicts, forgets or transposes something established earlier, which single-turn scoring has no way to see |
| **Whether a follow-up is answered without inventing detail never stated earlier** | The most consequential one. The model fills a gap in the conversation the same way it fills a gap in a document, and the invented detail now carries the authority of something the user believes they said |
| **Whether output quality holds as the conversation runs longer** | Degradation with accumulated context, which is the working-memory property of 2.2 arriving as a user-visible quality curve |

**The consequence for the dataset is the part teams underestimate: multi-turn evaluation needs its own golden dataset, and it is expensive.** The cases are full conversation transcripts with a known good response at each turn, covering the follow-ups, topic shifts and conversation lengths the system will actually see. A single-turn set cannot be adapted into one by concatenation, because what is being scored is the relationship between turns rather than the turns themselves.

**Scope it by whether the deployment is conversational at all.** A batch extraction pipeline does not need multi-turn evaluation. Any assistant a person talks to across more than one exchange does, and the absence of it is why so many systems score well and are described by their users as forgetting things.

### Three design principles

| Principle | The guidance |
| --- | --- |
| **Be task-specific** | Design evals that mirror your real-world task distribution. Do not forget edge cases |
| **Automate when possible** | Structure questions to allow automated grading: multiple choice, string match, code-graded, model-graded |
| **Prioritize volume over quality** | More questions with slightly lower signal automated grading is better than fewer questions with high-quality human hand-graded evals |

**The third is Anthropic's published guidance and it runs against the intuition**, so it is worth stating plainly rather than softening. It reconciles with task-specificity by dividing the work between them. **Task-specificity governs what is in the set**: mirror the real distribution and include edge cases deliberately, which is a design requirement. **Volume governs how many, given a choice between many automated and few manual.** If the trade-off is three hundred code-graded cases against thirty hand-graded ones, take the three hundred.

So the right answer to "our eval set is small because hand-grading is expensive" is **not** "keep it small and choose carefully". It is **automate the grading and expand the set.**

There is a practical route to volume: **have Claude generate more cases from a baseline set of examples**, and brainstorm eval methods with Claude where you do not know which apply. The caution worth keeping is that generated cases are good for representative coverage and weak for genuine edge cases, because the interesting edges are the ones nobody thought of, including the model.

### The three grader types

Code graders, model graders and human graders. **The robust pattern combines a code grader for validity with a model grader for quality**: the code grader answers whether the output is well formed, the model grader answers whether it is any good. The instruction that governs the choice is to take the fastest, most reliable and most scalable method that will serve.

| Grader type | Characterization | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Code-based** | **Fastest and most reliable, extremely scalable.** Lacks nuance for complex judgments requiring less rule-based rigidity | Exact match: `output == golden_answer`. String match: `key_phrase in output` |
| **Model-based** | Fast and flexible, scalable, suitable for complex judgment. **Test to ensure reliability first, then scale** | Likert scale, binary classification, ordinal scale |
| **Human** | Most flexible and highest quality, but slow and expensive. **Avoid if possible** | Manual review |

**Human grading is not a gold standard to scale toward.** Anthropic's documented position is that it is the most flexible and highest quality method but slow and expensive, and to avoid it where possible. Proposing to scale human review as the quality mechanism is the wrong move; automating the grader and reserving humans for calibration is the right one. Human review is expensive, finite and best spent where error is costly, which here means calibrating the automated grader and sampling production.

#### Three tips for model-based grading

1. **Have detailed, clear rubrics**, with automatic-fail conditions stated explicitly. The documentation's worked example: "The answer should always mention 'Acme Inc.' in the first sentence. If it does not, the answer is automatically graded as 'incorrect.'" A single criterion may need several rubrics for holistic evaluation.
2. **Be empirical or specific.** Instruct the grader to output only 'correct' or 'incorrect', or to judge on a 1 to 5 scale. Purely qualitative evaluation cannot be assessed quickly or at scale.
3. **Encourage reasoning.** Ask the grader to think first before deciding a score, **and then discard the reasoning.** This increases evaluation performance, particularly for tasks requiring complex judgment.

The third carries a refinement over the general advice about reasoning: the reasoning exists to improve the score and is then thrown away. It is a mechanism for better grading, not an artifact you keep.

#### Named eval methods

Exact match; string match; cosine similarity, for consistency; ROUGE-L, for summarization overlap; a model-graded Likert scale, for tone and style; model-graded binary classification, for privacy preservation; a model-graded ordinal scale, for context utilization. Recognizing which criterion a named method serves is most of the skill in using them.

### The loop

Write the prompt, build the dataset, run every case, grade, average into one number, change one thing, re-run, compare. A move from 3.9 to 7.9 is evidence. "It seems better now" is not.

### ⌂ The architect's lens

**The enterprise question this section does not ask.** Who agreed, before the work started, what score counts as a pass, and whether the party that builds the system may also be the party that certifies it.

**Governance at this decision.**

| Decision here | Governance decision that belongs with it | Artifact and owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Setting an acceptance threshold | What number is a pass, agreed in advance by a named business role | Signed acceptance criteria. Business sponsor |
| Building the eval set from real inputs | Provenance, lawful basis and access control for regulated data used as cases | Dataset register with an access list. Data owner |
| Automating the graders | Whether independent validation is required by policy regardless of the cost argument | Validation plan with an independence statement. Second line validation |

**What this costs the organization.** Advice to avoid human grading is first line efficiency guidance, and reading it as permission to drop independent review is how an evaluation program becomes unusable as evidence. The cost people forget is the human baseline: without the incumbent process's own error rate the score has no comparator, so the business case rests on a number with nothing to beat.

**The executive translation.** We agree the pass mark and who signs it before we build, and the team that builds the system will not be the team that certifies it.

## 8.3 The evaluation harness: what to build

**An evaluation harness is the component most often specified and least often built.** It appears in the design document, in the readiness pack and in the assurance narrative, and in a large proportion of systems it does not exist as a running thing. The consequence is that every quality claim downstream of it rests on an artifact nobody has seen produce a number. **A design review should ask to see the harness running rather than described**, on a real case set, with the score on screen. The distance between a harness that runs and a harness that is documented is invisible in a document and obvious in a demonstration.

### The minimum harness

- **Thirty to fifty cases**, including deliberate edge cases: ambiguous, malformed, empty, adversarial and cases where the information is genuinely absent from the source
- **A code grader** checking structural validity: parses, matches schema, required fields present, numbers reconcile
- **A model grader** producing strengths, weaknesses and reasoning **before** a score
- **A combined score**, and a single number per run
- **Two prompt versions**, so the comparison is run rather than asserted
- **Segment-level reporting**, because an aggregate number hides a failing segment and only the breakdown exposes it
- **Deliberate breakage**, treated below as its own step because it is the one most often skipped

### The deliberate breakage, which is what makes it an instrument

Make a required field of something the documents sometimes lack, and fabrication appears. Fix it and the metric moves. **A schema decision taken for tidiness at one end of the pipeline produces a fabrication failure at the other**, and one broken run establishes that connection in a way no description of it does. The second half matters as much as the first: an instrument that cannot show the repair is not yet an instrument, and a harness whose number does not move when a known defect is fixed is measuring something other than the defect.

### Harness reproducibility

A harness whose number moves for reasons nobody can name is not an instrument. Before one run can be compared to another, everything capable of moving the score other than the change under test has to be pinned and recorded.

| Pinned | Why a run is not comparable without it |
| --- | --- |
| **Model identifier and version** | The most common silent mover: a provider-initiated change arrives without a deployment on your side |
| **Sampling settings** | Temperature, top-p, maximum tokens, seed where available and the effort or thinking configuration. The last is the one omitted, and 8.5 already names it as a first suspect |
| **Dataset version** | A set that gained four cases between runs produced two scores over two populations |
| **Grader version, including the grader's own prompt and the model it runs on** | The instrument's own calibration. An edited rubric moves the score with nothing changed in the system, and it is the field least versioned |
| **Retrieval index snapshot** | An index rebuilt with different chunking is a behavior change of prompt magnitude, per the release tuple in 2.15 |
| **Code version** | Pre-processing, chunking, orchestration and the harness's own scoring arithmetic |

**The run manifest is the artifact carrying all of them, emitted by the run itself and stored beside the score.** Not a wiki page and not a commit message: a machine-readable record written at execution time, because one assembled afterward records what somebody believed was configured. A score without its manifest is a number with no provenance, and it cannot be used to defend a decision, reproduce a result or explain a divergence six months later.

**The harness is the only artifact in the system that must be more deterministic than the system it measures.** Everything that can be fixed is fixed, so the only variation surviving into the score is the model's own, which is the quantity being observed. A harness carrying its own non-determinism, in the form of a floating grader, a mutable set or an unpinned index, adds noise to the instrument and subtracts it from nothing.

An irreducible remainder is left, because the system under test is not deterministic and no pinning makes it so. The response is arithmetic: **run the unchanged system several times and report the spread alongside the mean, never a single figure.** The sizing method in 8.2 turns that spread into the noise floor deciding which differences count as results, and 8.6 gives the same quantity its comparative form as the self-disagreement floor. The mechanical consequence: the spread is an output of every run, and a harness reporting one number per run cannot produce it.

### Where the harness runs, and what it costs

A harness with one invocation point runs when somebody remembers. Four points, with different scopes and gates.

| Invocation | Scope | Gate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **On a pull request** | A fast subset | Blocking on a regression in the subset. Minutes, or it gets bypassed |
| **Nightly** | The full set | Non-blocking. Alerts on movement beyond the noise floor |
| **At a release gate** | The full set plus the hold-out | Blocking. The run the validation report is written from |
| **On any provider-initiated model change** | The full set, against both versions | Blocking on the new version. The artifact the model change row in 4.9 asks for |

**The pre-merge run has to be a subset for one reason: a check taking forty minutes will be bypassed.** The subset is chosen for its ability to fail rather than for its representativeness, which is the nightly run's job. Take every regression case, since each is a defect that already happened once; one case per segment reported on, so a segment-level break is visible rather than averaged away; the cases nearest the decision boundary, where a change lands first; and the adversarial cases, cheap to run and expensive to skip. A random sample is the wrong subset: it optimizes for the one property the subset does not need.

**A full run is a metered expense and belongs in the budget as a named line with an owner.** The arithmetic is cases times calls per case times tokens, plus the grader's own calls, routinely left out of the estimate and capable of exceeding the cost of the system under test wherever the rubric asks the grader to reason before scoring. Run nightly across a large set, that is a recurring bill against no feature.

⧉ **An unbudgeted harness gets switched off quietly, and that is the most common way evaluation stops.** It is never a decision to stop measuring. It is a cost review, a line nobody owns and a cadence reduced from nightly to weekly to on request, after which quality is asserted rather than known. Three defenses: fund it as part of the system rather than as a project cost, name its owner where the model spend is owned and keep the run cheap through prefix caching, the batch lane in 8.10 and a cheaper grader model held to the calibration obligation in 8.6.

Every run emits the same set: the manifest, the per-case scores with grader reasoning discarded, the segment breakdown, the aggregate with its spread and the pass or fail against the agreed threshold. Dated, retained and written where the operating team cannot edit it, that set is the evaluation artifact the evidence register in 4.9 requires. Its value is that the operation emits it rather than somebody assembling it before an inspection, the distinction between design-time and operating-effectiveness evidence.

### ⌂ The architect's lens

**The enterprise question this section does not ask.** What this harness produces that somebody outside engineering can read and sign, and who owns and funds it once the build team disperses.

**Governance at this decision.**

| Decision here | Governance decision that belongs with it | Artifact and owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Producing a combined score per run | A threshold agreed in advance and the role owning the pass or fail call | Dated validation report with a named signer. Business sponsor |
| Assembling thirty to fifty real cases | Where they came from, whether the data may be used this way and who may see the set | Dataset provenance record with an access list. Data owner |
| Building the model grader | Calibrating its agreement with human judgment before its scores are relied on | Calibration record with an agreement rate. Quality owner |

**What this costs the organization.** A harness that prints a number to a console cannot be handed to a sponsor, an audit function or a review board, so the work is repeated later in presentable form at a higher price. The cost people forget is maintaining the eval set: it ages with the corpus and the process, and an unmaintained set certifies the system against last year's reality.

**The executive translation.** The deliverable is a signed one page validation report carrying dataset version, prompt version and a segment breakdown, because that is the artifact a sponsor and a reviewer can both use.

## 8.4 Reliability engineering for non-deterministic systems

Classic reliability engineering assumes correctness is a deterministic function of the input, so the only interesting failure is the system not responding. **In an artificial intelligence system the responsive-and-wrong state is the dominant failure mode**, and it is invisible to every classic instrument. The discipline transfers; the indicator set does not.

### What is measurable and what is not

| Indicator | Measurable | Measurement lag | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Availability** | Yes, directly | Seconds | Includes third-party model dependency |
| **Latency** | Yes, directly | Seconds | As a distribution, never as a mean |
| **Throughput and rate-limit headroom** | Yes | Seconds | Peak matters, not average |
| **Task completion rate** | Yes | Minutes | The best cheap proxy for usefulness |
| **Escalation and override rate** | Yes | Minutes to hours | Leading quality indicator |
| **Quality** | Yes, but sampled and lagged | Hours to days | Requires grading. This is the whole problem |
| **Business outcome** | Partially | Weeks to quarters | Attribution is contestable |

**Quality is a service level indicator with a measurement lag, and the lag is the defining operational constraint of the discipline.** Availability is known now. Quality is known after a sample has been graded, which is hours at best. This means quality regressions run in production for a period no amount of monitoring removes, and it means the design must include a containment path that does not depend on knowing the answer yet.

```
   deploy        first bad      sample       graded      contained
     |            output          drawn       result         |
     |--------------|--------------|------------|------------|
     t0            t0+m          t0+h        t0+h+g        t0+c
                    \___________________________________/
                        THE EXPOSURE WINDOW
      shrink it with: canary %, online grading, guardrail
      metrics that move faster than quality (refusal rate,
      escalation rate, retrieval score distribution)
```

**Three fast proxies exist precisely because quality is slow: refusal rate, escalation rate and retrieval score distribution.** All three move within minutes and shift before a quality regression is measurable. They are not quality; they are the warning that quality is about to be measured badly.

### Latency, and why the mean is useless

For an agent run the mean is meaningless, because the distribution is a mixture: short runs resolved in one call, medium runs with two or three tool calls and long runs that looped. **Report p50, p90, p95 and p99 separately, segmented by task class and turn count.** A p99 that doubled while p50 stayed flat means the tail got longer, usually a retry loop or an agent failing to converge, and it is invisible in any average. Report time-to-first-token separately wherever a human is waiting, because perceived and actual latency are different commitments.

### Availability when the dependency is a third-party model

You cannot commit to availability you do not control. Three honest positions, in order of increasing engineering cost:

| Position | Commitment you can make | What it requires |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Pass-through** | Your availability is the provider's availability minus your own | Nothing. Disclose it |
| **Degraded mode** | Reduced capability remains available during provider unavailability | A defined degraded path: cached answers, a deterministic fallback, queue-and-retry or an honest "unavailable" with a human route |
| **Multi-provider or multi-region** | Higher availability at higher cost and complexity | Abstraction layer, per-provider evaluation and acceptance that quality differs across providers |

**The trap in the third row is quality equivalence.** Failing over preserves availability and changes behavior. An unevaluated fallback trades a visible outage for an invisible quality event, which is a worse trade in any regulated context.

### Error budgets applied to quality

The error budget transfers directly and is the most useful import from classic reliability engineering. Set a quality objective on a named population; the gap between it and one hundred percent is the budget. **Consumption of the budget by quality regressions governs change velocity**: while it is intact, ship changes; when it is exhausted, the only permitted changes are those that restore quality. This converts an argument about whether to slow down into an arithmetic fact, which is its entire value.

**Decision rule:** quality error budget exhausted means feature work stops and remediation starts, and this rule is agreed with the business owner before launch rather than negotiated during an incident.

### Writing the quality objective down

"Ninety-five percent accurate" is a number, not an objective. It cannot be missed, because nothing in it says on what, measured how, over what period or what follows. The error budget above is arithmetic performed on a quality objective, and on a bare percentage it yields nothing. 8.8 sets out what a commitment to a business owner must carry; this is the internal engineering form, and it adds the instrument and the window.

| Part | The question it answers | What a bare percentage leaves open |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Population** | Which requests this applies to | Scope, so every disagreement about a miss becomes an argument about scope |
| **Instrument and cadence** | What measures it, how often | The number is whatever was last computed by whoever computed it |
| **Window** | Over what period it is assessed | A bad afternoon and a bad quarter are the same event |
| **Action on a miss** | What happens, and who does it | A negotiation during an incident, at the worst time with the worst information |

In operable form: field-level extraction correctness of at least 94 percent on standard-form invoices from the top forty suppliers, measured by the code grader plus the calibrated model grader on two hundred sampled production cases a week, over a rolling four-week window, with a miss stopping feature work and routing the segment to full review until two windows clear.

**The population clause is the one that gets dropped, and the one carrying the risk.** A system at ninety-five percent overall can be at ninety-nine percent on the routine eighty percent of traffic and seventy percent on the segment where the consequential decisions sit. The objective is met, the reporting is honest and the segment is failing entirely. Stating the population forces the objective to be written per segment, or to name the excluded segments and where those cases route: the same discipline the per-segment case floor in 8.2 imposes on the eval set.

**The objective is a commitment, so its rigor moves with the tier per 4.2.** At T1 one objective over the whole population, self-certified by the owner. At T2 a defined instrument and a review cadence. At T3 objectives per affected group, on the segmentation the tier's evaluation rigor requires, with misses reported at governance review. At T4 the same, with the instrument operated by a party that did not build the system.

When the number drops, localize in a fixed order.

1. **The harness.** A grader prompt edit, a dataset change or an unpinned index moves the score with nothing wrong in the system, and it is the only candidate that can make the drop unreal.
2. **The model version.** One fact, answerable from the logged version field, and the change most likely to have arrived with nobody doing anything.
3. **The prompt version.** Also one logged fact, and the change your team most recently made.
4. **The corpus.** Slower to check, much larger and changed through publication workflows that never touch the pipeline, per 8.6.
5. **The traffic mix.** Slowest, and the case where nothing is wrong: the population moved, which is user drift in 8.5 and calls for onboarding, not a model change.

**The order is not arbitrary.** It runs from the cheapest check with the highest chance of a false alarm to the most expensive with the highest chance of no defect at all, and the harness comes first because everything after it assumes the measurement is sound. Inverting the order is how a team spends two weeks reindexing a corpus to fix an edited grader prompt.

### The honest conversation with a business owner

Four things you can commit to and one you cannot. You can commit to **availability**, on whichever of the three positions above you have actually taken and disclosed, to **latency percentiles**, to **a measured quality level on a named population with a defined routing rule for the remainder** and to **a response procedure when quality misses**. You cannot commit to correctness on any individual case. Saying so early is the difference between a defensible agreement and an argument in month four where the vendor says the system was up and the client says it was wrong.

## 8.5 Monitoring, observability and drift

### The six monitoring layers

**Six layers, each answering a different question for a different audience.** A monitoring design that stops at the first three, which most do, will report a healthy system that is producing wrong answers.

```
  6 GOVERNANCE  policy violations, disclosure, human gate use
     ^          audience: risk, compliance, audit
  5 BUSINESS    outcome, adoption, cycle time, deflection
     ^          audience: sponsor, business owner
  4 QUALITY     correctness, groundedness, override rate
     ^          audience: quality owner, architect
  3 MODEL       tokens, cache hits, refusals, stop reasons,
     ^          effort config, model version
  2 INTEGRATION tool errors, retrieval scores, connector health
     ^
  1 INFRA       availability, latency, rate limits, queues
                audience for 1 to 3: operations
```

| Layer | Alert on | Merely chart |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Infrastructure** | Availability breach, rate-limit rejection, queue depth growth, p99 latency breach | Request volume, regional split |
| **Integration** | Tool error rate above threshold, connector auth failure, index staleness beyond commitment, retrieval returning empty | Retrieval score distribution, tool call mix |
| **Model** | Refusal rate step change, cache hit ratio collapse, unexpected model version in traffic | Token mix, effort distribution, output length |
| **Quality** | Sampled correctness below threshold, override rate step change, groundedness drop | Per-segment accuracy, citation accuracy |
| **Business outcome** | Nothing. Outcomes move too slowly to page anyone | Adoption, completion, cycle time, deflection |
| **Governance** | Human gate bypassed, policy-violating output detected, access anomaly | Gate volumes, review latency, disclosure acknowledgment |

**The alerting rule: alert only on conditions with a defined response.** An alert with no runbook entry trains the on-call engineer to ignore alerts, which costs more than the alert was worth. Everything else is a chart reviewed on a cadence.

### Observability and the minimum capture set

Observability is the ability to answer questions about a running system without redeploying it. At scale that requires having decided in advance what to capture, because the question you need answered arrives after the request it concerns has gone.

| Capture | Why |
| --- | --- |
| **Correlation identifier** tying every step of one logical request together across model calls, tool calls and agents | Without it, multi-step systems are undebuggable. The most important item here |
| **Prompt version and model identifier**, with effort and thinking configuration | When quality changes this is the first thing you want and the most commonly missing. Effort belongs in this set |
| **The three token fields**: `input_tokens`, `cache_creation_input_tokens`, `cache_read_input_tokens` | They bill at 1x, 1.25x and 0.1x respectively. Note that `input_tokens` counts **only tokens after the last cache breakpoint**, so total input is the sum of all three. Getting this wrong understates usage |
| **Latency as a distribution**: median, p95, p99 and time-to-first-token separately | Averages hide the tail, and the tail is what users complain about |
| **Tool calls, arguments and outcomes**, with error categories | Tells you what the system actually did |
| **Retrieval detail**: what was retrieved, with scores, and whether the answer used it | Retrieval quality is invisible unless logged, and it is the most common cause of confident wrong answers |
| **Error categories** distinguishing transient, validation, business-rule and permission failures | Each implies a different response |
| **Stop reasons and refusals** | The platform distinguishes these; a rising refusal rate is an over-restriction signal |
| **Cost per request and per completed outcome** | The second is the number that matters |
| **Human overrides and corrections** | Free labeled examples and the cheapest quality signal available |

**The single most important item in the set is the correlation identifier.** Without it anything above the fourth rung of the complexity ladder is undebuggable, and the sharp rise in observability requirement from the fifth rung upward consists precisely of this.

### System failures, quality failures and why silence is not health

System failures and quality failures need different instrumentation. A crashed request appears in the logs. A fluent, well-formatted, confidently wrong answer does not. **Logs tell you the system ran; only evaluation and sampled human review tell you it was right.** An observability design that monitors error rates and latency alone is incomplete for an artificial intelligence system.

**An artificial intelligence system fails by producing a plausible wrong answer, and a plausible wrong answer generates no error, no exception, no latency anomaly and no log line distinguishable from a correct one.** Three consequences follow, all design requirements rather than good practice.

1. **Absence of errors is not evidence of health.** Health is evidenced by sampled grading, not by a clean dashboard.
2. **The high-confidence population must be sampled.** Nobody checks it, so a new failure mode survives there longest.
3. **Distribution shift is alertable; hard failure alone is not sufficient.** Degradation is gradual and silent, so the alert goes on the shape of the traffic rather than the failures in it.

**Decision rule:** if your monitoring would look identical during a week in which the system answered every question confidently and wrongly, you are not monitoring an artificial intelligence system.

### Observability at scale

Four strategies once volume makes full capture impractical. Sample rather than capture everything, but stratify so rare categories are represented. Keep full traces for every error and a random slice of successes. Aggregate by segment, since one overall accuracy number hides total failure on one document type. And put the alerts on distribution shift.

**The shift signals worth alerting on: refusal rate, output length, retrieval score distribution, escalation rate, tool-error rate and cache hit ratio.** The last is both a cost signal and an early warning that something in the prompt prefix has started changing.

**The compliance overlay.** Logs contain inputs and outputs, which frequently means they contain regulated personal data. Retention, access control and redaction are part of the observability design rather than an afterthought to it.

**And the capture set above is not an audit log.** It is built for diagnosis, which makes it sampled, mutable, aggregation-optimized and retained for weeks. The record an auditor, a regulator or opposing counsel reads is the separate immutable set in 4.8, which shares most of these fields and none of these properties. A team that has built this set has built observability and nothing else, and 4.8 names believing otherwise as the most common finding in assurance work. The two are separable at storage even where they share an emission path.

### Drift: five kinds, five detections

**Drift is the reason a system that passed every test at launch is wrong a year later with nothing changed in the code.**

| Drift | What moved | Detection | Typical response |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Input drift** | The questions users ask changed | Query embedding distribution, new-term frequency, intent classification mix | Extend the eval set; check coverage on the new intents |
| **Output drift** | Responses changed shape without an input change | Length distribution, refusal rate, format compliance, sentiment | Investigate as a model or config change first |
| **Behavior drift on model upgrade** | The provider's model changed under you | **Shadow evaluation before cutover**, then paired comparison after | Re-tune prompt; re-baseline; do not assume improvement |
| **Corpus drift** | Documents added, edited or expired | Document count and age distribution, continuous labeled retrieval evaluation, freshness monitor | Re-run retrieval evaluation; check governance expiry |
| **User drift** | The population using it changed | Cohort mix, seniority mix, tenure of active users | Re-segment quality; new cohorts frequently have lower success |

**User drift is the one always missed.** The pilot cohort was volunteers who were trained, motivated and forgiving; the general population is none of those. Measured quality falls after general availability with no technical change whatsoever, and the correct response is onboarding rather than a model change.

### Diagnosis: symptom to first suspect

**Classify the failure before attributing it.** Instrumentation reports that a metric moved. It does not say what kind of failure moved it, and the four classes below take four different fixes, so naming the class first is what stops a team applying the wrong one confidently.

| Class | What it is | Where the fix lives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Prompt failure** | The instruction was ambiguous or underspecified and the model filled the gap | The prompt. Not the model, and not the model tier |
| **Hallucination** | Confident fluent content not grounded in the input or any reliable source | Grounding: retrieval, tool use or verification. **Stronger instruction will not resolve it**, which is the most commonly attempted wrong fix |
| **Model mismatch** | The tier is wrong for the task, or the version was swapped without re-evaluation | Model selection, gated by an eval |
| **Orchestrator-workers failure** | In a multi-agent run, a recoverable subagent failure and an unrecoverable orchestrator failure present alike from the outside | Attribution requires a trace spanning both, which is what the shared trace identifier of 2.4 exists for |

The second row is the one worth marking, because the wrong fix for a hallucination is so intuitive: the output is wrong, the instruction seems to have been ignored, so the instruction is made more emphatic. Emphasis does not supply a fact the model does not have.

Having named the class, map the symptom to the component that could have produced it, weighted toward whatever changed most recently.

| Symptom | First suspect |
| --- | --- |
| Confident wrong answers beginning at a content update, model and latency unchanged | **Retrieval and indexing** |
| Output format wrong or inconsistent | The prompt or the output contract. Enforce a schema; prefill; add examples |
| Fields fabricated that are absent from the source | **A required schema field that should be optional.** A required field forces invention |
| Identical inputs producing different answers | Non-determinism, or more often criteria vague enough that several answers are defensible |
| Quality degrading over a long conversation | Context management: accumulated clutter, summarization erosion, key facts lost from the middle |
| Failure concentrated in one document type or field | Data-shape mismatch. Check accuracy by segment before concluding anything general |
| Quality dropped after a model or version change | Model mismatch, or a prompt coupled tightly to the old model's quirks |
| Quality dropped after a config change with no model change | **Effort or thinking configuration.** Easy to miss |
| Numbers wrong, everything else right | The model was asked to do arithmetic. Move computation into code |
| Answers correct but unsupported by the citation | Attribution not preserved through the pipeline |
| Refusing valid requests | Over-restrictive guardrails or a badly tuned screen. **A defect, not caution** |
| Cost rising with no change in volume | Context growth, **cache invalidation** or retry loops |
| Cache writes on every request and no reads | The breakpoint sits on a block that changes each request |
| Agent takes many turns and finishes nothing | No ground truth from the environment; the agent cannot assess its own progress |
| Agent picks the wrong tool with a large catalog | Tool selection degradation past 30 to 50 loaded tools, or overlapping descriptions |
| Everything looks fine and users are unhappy | You are measuring the wrong thing. Go and watch someone use it |

Two habits: reproduce before theorizing, and change one variable at a time.

**And the trap: aggregate accuracy deceives.** Ninety-seven percent overall can mask complete failure on one document type or field. Always segment before deciding that a system is healthy or that human review can be reduced.

### ⌂ The architect's lens

**The enterprise question this section does not ask.** Traces hold full inputs and outputs aggregated across every system a request touched, which often makes them the most sensitive store in the deployment. Who may read them, and for how long.

**Governance at this decision.**

| Decision here | Governance decision that belongs with it | Artifact and owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Defining the minimum capture set | Classification, retention and access group decided per field before capture | Log classification and retention schedule. Data protection officer |
| Capturing inputs, outputs and retrieved sources | Which fields are operational telemetry and which are the record of an interaction | Two retention regimes with two access groups. Service owner with the records manager |
| Running an online test on live traffic | Whether experimenting on customers is permitted, and whether it must be disclosed | Experiment approval record. Compliance |

**What this costs the organization.** An engineering retention default of a few weeks against a business record kept for years means rebuilding the record of what happened fails at the moment it is finally needed. The cost people forget is the access model: traces aggregate content from separately entitled systems, so the trace store can grant in one place what every source system separately denies.

**The executive translation.** The logs are a regulated data store in their own right, so we set classification, retention and access before we decide what to capture.

## 8.6 Continuous evaluation and controlled comparison

Evaluation as a launch artifact is a photograph. **Evaluation as a running control is the instrument that keeps the system honest**, and the transition between the two is the highest-value operational move available after launch.

| Instrument | Cadence | Purpose | Failure it catches |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Regression suite** | Every change, blocking | Nothing that worked stopped working | Change-induced regression |
| **Golden set** | Every change and weekly | Absolute quality against known-correct answers | Slow degradation |
| **Labeled retrieval set** | Daily or continuous | Retrieval quality independent of generation | Corpus drift, index staleness |
| **Online sampling with grading** | Continuous, stratified | Real-traffic quality with real distribution | Everything the offline sets did not anticipate |
| **Human review sample** | Weekly, stratified | Grader calibration and novel failure discovery | Judge drift, unknown failure modes |
| **Shadow evaluation** | Before every model or major dependency change | Behavior comparison at zero user risk | Behavior drift on upgrade |

**Golden set maintenance is a governed activity.** Add, never quietly edit, because editing breaks comparability across the whole history. Every fixed production failure enters permanently and every new segment gets representation before it goes live. The one legitimate modification is a case whose correct answer changed because the policy changed, and it is logged.

**Sampling rates.** Stratify rather than sample uniformly, because uniform sampling spends the review budget on the common case. A workable default: full capture for errors and escalations, a meaningful rate for low-confidence outputs, a smaller rate for high-confidence outputs and full capture for any thin segment. **The high-confidence stratum is not optional**, and dropping it to save budget removes the only instrument pointed at the failure mode that matters most.

### Controlled comparison: offline first, online second

**Offline comparison.** Same dataset, two versions, compare. Change one thing at a time, hold the dataset constant, look for regressions in the categories you were not trying to improve, and re-run rather than reasoning about whether the change should have helped.

**Online comparison on live traffic.** Split traffic between versions and compare real outcomes. This remains necessary because offline evaluation measures what you thought to measure and production surfaces what you did not. A sound online test needs six things: a primary metric decided in advance; a stopping rule; guardrail metrics that halt it regardless of the primary result; a rollback path that does not require a deployment; segment-level reporting; and enough traffic to distinguish the effect from noise.

**Sequence matters: offline first, online second.** Putting a change in front of users to find out whether it works is expensive when the harness would have told you for nothing.

#### The statistics an online test cannot skip

Online comparison is A/B testing, and the discipline it requires is the one A/B testing has always required, with one addition specific to non-deterministic systems.

**Decide the sample size before the test starts.** The size follows from three numbers: the baseline rate of the primary metric, the smallest improvement that would change the decision and the variability of the measure. Skip the calculation and one of two things happens. The test is underpowered, returns no significant difference, and the change is abandoned although it worked. Or the test runs until a difference appears, which is guaranteed eventually and means nothing.

**The peeking problem is the one that catches experienced teams.** Checking the result repeatedly and stopping when it turns significant inflates the false-positive rate far above the nominal threshold, because each look is another chance for noise to cross the line. The remedy is a stopping rule fixed in advance: a target sample size, or an explicitly sequential design whose thresholds already account for repeated looks. A dashboard that anyone can watch continuously is a peeking machine, and the discipline has to be procedural because the dashboard will not enforce it.

**Segment reporting multiplies the comparisons.** Reporting one primary metric across twelve segments is twelve tests, and at a conventional threshold roughly one will look significant by chance. Nominate the primary metric and the primary segment in advance; treat every other segment as exploratory, generating hypotheses for the next test rather than conclusions for this one.

**Control the input distribution across arms, not only the assignment.** Random assignment of requests distributes inputs evenly in expectation and does not do so in any particular test, and at small samples the gap between those two statements is where false results live. Where the input population is heterogeneous, and a document corpus ranging from a few pages to many is the ordinary case, an arm can receive materially fewer hard cases than the other and return an improvement that is an artifact of routing. Stratify the assignment on whatever dimension drives difficulty, and report the composition of each arm alongside the result. **An unreported arm composition is an uncheckable result**, because the reader cannot distinguish a better version from an easier sample.

**The addition for non-deterministic systems is the self-disagreement floor.** Before comparing two versions, measure how much the *same* version disagrees with itself across runs on the same inputs. That figure is the floor beneath which no comparison is meaningful, and it is frequently larger than the effect being tested. 2.15 develops the method under shadow and canary deployment; the point here is that it belongs at the design of the test, not at the interpretation of the result.

**Where traffic is scarce, the design changes rather than the standard.** A low-volume workflow will not accumulate the sample a clean split needs in any useful period. The honest options are to lengthen the window and accept the delay, to test on a proxy metric that moves faster while validating the proxy against the outcome metric separately, or to abandon the online test and rely on offline comparison plus staged rollout with tight monitoring. The dishonest option, which is common, is to run the underpowered test anyway and present the result as evidence.

#### The interaction effect classical A/B testing does not have

There is one failure mode specific to these systems and it is temporal rather than statistical. **A change that improves performance on typical inputs can degrade performance on an input class that is rare during the test window and common later.** Nothing in the arithmetic catches this, because within the window the rare class contributes too few observations to move any metric, and the result is correctly computed and wrong about the future.

The usual shape is seasonal.
