A workload whose input mix shifts at a quarter end, a filing deadline, an enrolment period or a renewal cycle will run its experiment against one distribution and its production life against several. **Test-period and input-distribution alignment matters more here than in most software experiments**, and the practical discipline is to state, alongside the result, which input classes the window under-represented and to treat the change as unvalidated on those classes rather than validated overall. Where a known spike is coming, the alternatives are to run the test through it or to hold the rare classes out and score them offline against the golden set.

#### Shadow testing as an experimental posture, not only a release step

Shadow deployment appears in 2.15 and 8.5 as a step in a release sequence. It is also a **choice of experiment design**, and it is the right one more often than teams assume.

**The mechanism.** Run the candidate in parallel with the incumbent, send it a copy of live requests, and serve every user the incumbent's response. The candidate's outputs are logged rather than returned and scored offline afterward. **The deployment decision is made before a single user has seen the new version**, which is the whole of its value.

| | Live split | Shadow |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **User exposure to a worse version** | Bounded but real. Some fraction of users receive the regression before the test closes | None |
| **What you can measure** | Real user behavior, including downstream signals a live response produces: acceptance, follow-up, escalation, abandonment | Output quality only, scored against an offline rubric or golden answers |
| **What decides its use** | The deployment can absorb bounded exposure, and traffic is high enough to reach a meaningful sample in a usable window | A single bad output carries too much risk, or traffic is too low to support a split before the change is needed |

**The cost of shadow testing is the loss of downstream signal, and it is a real cost rather than a technicality.** Whether a user accepted the answer, and what they did next, is frequently the only measure of task success that means anything, and no shadow run produces it. Scoring falls back to the rubric, which measures what you thought to measure.

⚠ **In a regulated deployment, the choice may already be made.** Where exposing users to an unvalidated model change is not permissible, shadow testing is not the conservative option among two, it is the only admissible way to validate the change, and the experiment design has to accept rubric-based scoring as the ceiling. Name that constraint before designing the test rather than after the compliance review rejects the split.

### Five iteration techniques

1. **Concrete input and output examples** communicate a transformation better than description
2. **Test-first.** Define expected behavior including edge cases before building
3. **Have the system interview you.** Before building in an unfamiliar domain, having the model ask questions surfaces design considerations while they are still cheap
4. **Batch interacting problems, sequence independent ones.** If fixing one affects another, present them together; if they are independent, take them one at a time
5. **Recycle your best outputs as examples** in the next version

### Judge calibration and the evaluation of the evaluator

A model grader is a system in production with all the properties of one, and it is almost never monitored as such. **Three obligations.**

**Calibrate before trusting.** Grade a set with humans, grade it with the judge and measure agreement. Report agreement per class, not overall accuracy, because a judge agreeing ninety percent overall may agree twenty percent on the rare failure class that is the entire reason you built it.

**Monitor for judge drift.** The judge's model changes, its prompt gets edited, the traffic moves. Re-run a frozen calibration set on a schedule and alert on movement. **A judge whose scores drift makes every trend line above it meaningless, including the ones used to justify the last three changes.**

**Watch the two structural biases.** Model graders reward fluency and length independently of correctness, and they are lenient toward outputs from the same model family. Both are correctable in the rubric and neither is correctable by hoping.

**Decision rule:** any metric produced by a model grader is reported with the date of its last human calibration attached, and an uncalibrated judge score is not admissible evidence for a change.

### The change-management link

**No prompt, model, tool, corpus or guardrail change ships without an eval run.** All five, and the corpus change is the one omitted everywhere. Corpus changes are made by content owners who are not engineers, through publication workflows that never touch the deployment pipeline, and they change behavior as thoroughly as a prompt edit does. A change policy that governs code and leaves the corpus ungoverned has left the largest surface uncontrolled.

| Change type | Minimum gate | Who approves |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Prompt** | Regression suite plus golden set, offline before online | Quality owner |
| **Model or version** | Shadow evaluation, then canary with guardrail metrics, accepted per segment rather than in aggregate | Quality owner and business owner |
| **Tool added or scope widened** | Security review plus regression suite | Security owner |
| **Corpus publication** | Validation gate plus labeled retrieval set | Knowledge owner |
| **Guardrail or threshold** | Regression suite plus false-refusal measurement | Quality owner |

### The experiment-design plane

The statistics above tell you how to run a test correctly. **A prior question decides whether this change deserves a test at all and what posture the test should take**, and it resolves on two axes: the effect size you expect and the confidence you need before acting on the result.

| | **Small expected effect** | **Large expected effect** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **High confidence required** | The most expensive quadrant. A small effect measured to a high standard needs a large sample and a long window. Where the stakes justify it, run it properly or do not run it. Where they do not, reconsider whether the change is worth making | Test properly and expect a short window. A large effect reaches significance quickly, and the confidence requirement is met by the design rather than by duration |
| **Moderate confidence acceptable** | Staged rollout with monitoring is usually the better instrument than a formal split. The test would cost more than the decision is worth | A short split test with a pre-specified primary metric. The effect is visible fast and the standard is proportionate |
| **Low confidence acceptable** | Do not run a test. Ship it behind the regression suite and watch the guardrail metrics. A formal experiment on a low-stakes change with a small expected effect consumes the traffic budget a real question will need | Not a real position. If the effect is large enough to matter, the confidence requirement is not low |

**Placement is a judgment about consequence, not about interest.** A wording change to a clarification message in a low-stakes assistant is a small effect where low confidence is acceptable, and it does not deserve an experiment. A prompt architecture change in a system whose error could delay clinical treatment sits at high confidence whatever the expected effect size, and the sample requirement follows from the consequence rather than from the change's apparent size. A new classification category expected to capture a large share of incoming volume is a large effect and reaches a verdict quickly. A model tier substitution proposed for cost saving is a two-sided test: the cost effect is large and certain, so the question under test is whether quality degrades, and the primary metric is the quality one.

**Traffic scarcity moves the design, not the standard.** A change to a workflow processing a couple of hundred requests a day will not accumulate a usable sample in any useful window, and the honest response is offline comparison plus staged rollout with tight monitoring rather than an underpowered split presented as evidence.

⧉ **The quadrant is decided before the test and reported with the result.** A result presented without the posture that produced it invites the reader to assume the strongest one, and the most common way an experiment misleads is not a bad calculation but a moderate-confidence design read as a high-confidence finding.


## 8.7 Metrics and value attribution

A metrics list is a dashboard nobody reads. **A metrics architecture is four levels, each answering to a different audience on a different clock.**

| Level | Question | Named metrics | Clock | Audience |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1 System health** | Is it running? | Availability, p95 and p99 latency, error rate by class, rate-limit headroom, cost per request | Minutes | Operations |
| **2 Quality** | Is it right? | Correctness by segment, groundedness, citation accuracy, override rate, escalation rate, false refusal rate, task completion rate | Hours to days | Quality owner |
| **3 Adoption** | Is it used, by whom, for what? | Weekly active users as a share of eligible, tasks per active user, repeat use rate, share of eligible work processed, abandonment rate | Weeks | Business owner |
| **4 Business outcome** | Did it change anything that matters? | Cycle time, cost per case, throughput per person, quality of the end product, deflection rate, revenue or loss effect | Quarters | Sponsor |

**Leading and lagging.** Levels 1 and 2 lead; levels 3 and 4 lag. **Override rate is the single most useful leading indicator in the set**, because users generate it while doing their job and it moves within hours where the level 4 measures move over quarters. It leads on quality rather than on outcome generally: a degradation arriving through a change in the surrounding process moves level 4 without ever touching the override rate, so a flat override rate is evidence about the system and not about the deployment. Repeat use rate is the best leading indicator of level 4, and people who tried the system twice and stopped are the most informative population in the deployment and the one nobody interviews.

### The vanity metrics to refuse

| Metric | Why it is refused | What to report instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Number of queries** | Measures activity, not value. Rises when the system is unhelpful and people re-ask | Task completion rate, repeat use rate |
| **Tokens consumed** | A cost input reported as an achievement | Cost per completed outcome |
| **Seats provisioned** | Measures procurement, not adoption | Weekly active users as a share of eligible users |
| **Documents indexed** | Measures ingestion, not coverage | Coverage per knowledge domain |
| **Model calls per day** | Rises with inefficiency | Calls per completed task |

**Refusing these is a professional obligation and it will be unpopular**, because they rise reliably and are already on somebody's slide. The argument that works: each also rises when the system gets worse, which makes them unusable as evidence.

### Attribution, honestly

The business will ask what the system delivered and the honest answer has bounds. **Four attribution methods, in descending order of strength.** Name which one you used.

| Method | Strength | Cost | When it is available |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Randomized holdout** | Strongest | Moderate, plus the political cost of withholding a benefit | Large user populations, divisible work |
| **Staged rollout with comparison** | Strong | Low | Any phased deployment. The realistic default |
| **Pre and post with controls** | Moderate | Low | Stable processes with a clean baseline |
| **Self-reported time saved** | Weak | Very low | Directional only. Never present alone |

**The limit to state out loud: an artificial intelligence system deployed into a process that also changed in other ways cannot be cleanly attributed, and claiming otherwise damages credibility for every subsequent claim.** Report the measured effect, name the method, name the confounders and say what would have been needed to isolate it. What sponsors do not respect is a benefits case that collapses under one question.

### Worked measurement plan: contract review assistant in procurement

The use case: an assistant that reviews inbound supplier contracts against a clause playbook, flags deviations and drafts a summary for a contract manager. Volume approximately four hundred contracts per month. Built before launch, which is the only time it can be built.

| Element | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| **Primary business objective** | Reduce time from contract receipt to first substantive response, without increasing missed non-standard clauses |
| **Baseline, measured before launch** | Median 6.2 working days receipt to first response, from twelve months of case records. Missed non-standard clause rate 4.1 percent, from a manual audit of a random sample of one hundred completed reviews |
| **Level 1 metrics** | Availability, p95 latency per contract, cost per contract reviewed |
| **Level 2 metrics** | Clause detection recall against a labeled set of two hundred contracts, segmented by clause type; false flag rate; groundedness of the summary; contract manager override rate |
| **Level 3 metrics** | Share of eligible contracts processed through the assistant; repeat use by contract manager; abandonment rate mid-review |
| **Level 4 metrics** | Median receipt-to-first-response time; missed non-standard clause rate on audit; contracts per manager per month |
| **Attribution method** | Staged rollout by region. Two regions live in month one, two held back to month four, compared on the level 4 metrics |
| **Guardrail metrics** | Missed non-standard clause rate must not exceed baseline. This halts the rollout regardless of the time saving |
| **Segments reported separately** | Clause type, contract value band, counterparty jurisdiction, contract manager tenure |
| **Decision point** | Month four. Continue, remediate or stop, against pre-agreed thresholds |
| **Who reads what** | Operations reads level 1 daily; quality owner reads level 2 weekly; business owner reads level 3 monthly; sponsor reads level 4 at the decision point |

**Three features make this a plan rather than a dashboard.** The baseline was measured before launch, the step that is skipped and cannot be recovered afterward. The guardrail metric can stop the rollout on its own regardless of the primary result. And the decision point has a date and three named outcomes agreed in advance, so the month-four conversation is an evaluation rather than a negotiation.

**Decision rule:** if the baseline was not measured before launch, the value question is permanently unanswerable, so measure it or agree in writing that value will not be claimed.

### The value statement: from a feasible design to a defensible number

Attribution above answers what the system delivered once it is running. **The value statement answers a different question asked earlier and by a different person: whether building it is worth doing at all**, and it is the artifact that travels alongside the feasibility verdict of 2.2 into the scope document. A feasibility verdict tells the business owner the system can be built inside the budget and the constraints. It does not tell them it should be.

**Five pillars carry the business case**, and naming which one a claim advances keeps the conversation in the language the sponsor already uses.

| Pillar | The claim it supports |
| --- | --- |
| **Efficiency** | The same work done faster or cheaper |
| **Transformation** | Work that was not feasible before becoming possible |
| **Productivity** | More output from the same people |
| **Solution cost** | The run cost of the system itself, which is a negative line and belongs in the same table |
| **Performance service levels** | The service levels the deployment has to hold, which are a constraint on the other four rather than a benefit |

Map each claim to the pillar it advances, so the value statement captures both the number and the kind of value it represents. A claim that cannot be assigned to a pillar is usually a feature description wearing a benefit's clothing.

**The mechanism is a comparison between two states, and the mapping is built in four steps.** Each step has to land on a number the business owner will recognize.

1. **Name the baseline in a business unit.** Start from how the task is performed today and measure it in the unit the business already tracks: analyst hours per case, average days to resolution, cases per person per month. The baseline must come from the business owner's own operational data. A baseline pulled from intuition produces a figure no finance team will accept, and the error stays hidden until somebody asks for its source, at which point the whole case is rebuilt.
2. **Predict the post-deployment state in the same unit.** Where the feasibility verdict requires a human review gate, the projection has to include that cost. Routing low-confidence output to a reviewer reduces labor. It does not eliminate it, and projecting full automation against a design that specifies human review overstates the value by exactly the amount operations will later reject.
3. **Subtract the run cost from the sizing model.** Take the projected monthly cost produced during sizing and treat it as the recurring cost of the new state. Build cost is handled separately in step 4. Reusing the sizing output keeps the two analyses consistent: a change to the token budget or the model tier then updates the cost ceiling and the value case together, rather than leaving them to drift apart.
4. **State the payback period and the sensitivity.** Express the result as the time for the accumulated operational gain to cover the build cost and the run cost. Then state how that period moves if the volume assumptions or the gain-per-task assumptions are wrong. A payback period quoted without sensitivity invites a decision based on a single optimistic scenario, which is the scenario that fails first when the system meets real volumes.

**Three errors account for most unusable value cases.**

| Error | Why it happens and where it surfaces |
| --- | --- |
| **The baseline is estimated rather than measured** | The business owner does not have clean operational data, so the baseline is filled in from intuition. The apparent gain is misleading, and the error stays hidden until finance asks for the source of the baseline number during business case review |
| **The projection assumes full automation when the design requires human review** | The value case models reduced labor as eliminated labor. The gap surfaces in the first operational period after launch, when actual analyst hours fail to fall as far as the case promised |
| **The run cost is taken from an average rather than the sizing distribution** | Using an average token cost instead of the distribution understates the recurring cost, which overstates net value. It concentrates on workflows with heavy-tailed inputs, where a small fraction of large requests drives most of the cost |

**The output is a short value statement handed to the business owner alongside the feasibility verdict.** It ties the answers to "can we build this" and "is it worth building" back to numbers the business already owns, and the two artifacts travel together into the statement of work.

**The dashboard equivalent of this discipline is the translation layer.** The people who funded the deployment are not reading the request-level trace. They are reading a measure of the outcome the deployment was meant to improve, so the observability stack needs a mapping from the technical metrics to the business metrics they drive: task success rate to first-contact resolution, latency to handle time. **Build that mapping when the system is designed, not after the first business review**, because a mapping absent at build time turns the first review question into a retrospective reconstruction rather than a live query.


## 8.8 Feedback loops and continuous improvement

The loop is an operating routine, not a value. **A routine requires three things: a cadence, a named owner and a queue.** Without all three it is a set of good intentions that decays within two months of launch, which is the observed fate of most of them.

```
   SIGNAL           TRIAGE          BACKLOG        SHIP
   failures    ->   classify   ->  prioritized  -> change +
   overrides        instance        by impact      eval run
   escalations      or class?       x effort           |
   user feedback        |                              |
   query gaps           +-- instance -> fix + add       |
   eval results         |              to eval set      |
   incidents            +-- class ----> root cause      |
        ^                                               |
        |                                               v
        +----------- CLOSE THE LOOP WITH THE USER -------+
              "you reported X, here is what changed"
```

| Signal source | What it tells you | Volume | Bias or caveat |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Failures and errors** | Hard defects | Low | None, but misses the dangerous failures |
| **Human overrides and corrections** | Quality defects, with the correct answer attached | High | Cheapest and most valuable signal available |
| **Escalations** | Where the boundary of competence sits | Medium | Reflects routing rules as much as capability |
| **User feedback** | Perceived quality, and what users expected | Low and falling | Heavily biased to negative and to vocal users |
| **Query gaps** | Content the corpus lacks | High | The content backlog. Routes outside engineering |
| **Eval results** | Regression and drift | Fixed by cadence | Only measures what you thought to measure |
| **Incidents** | Systemic weakness | Rare | Highest information per unit |

### The governance table: which signals reach whom, and which fire on a calendar

The loop above is an engineering routine and it improves the system. **A second table decides which signals leave the team**, and it is a different artifact with a different owner. Observability collects. The loop triages. **Neither of them decides that a stakeholder needs to know**, and that gap is where the characteristic failure of this section lives.

The failure has a shape worth recognizing in a record. Over a ninety-day window, eval scores drift down week over week from week four. Error rates stay flat, so no hard alert fires. No review is scheduled, because reviews are quarterly. In week twelve the quarterly review finally surfaces it, and by then the stakeholder has already noticed that the output is "less useful lately". **Every signal the deployment needed was collected from week four onward. Nothing in the design decided that any of them mattered.** A drift with no trigger is invisible until a person happens to notice, and the stack was measuring the right thing and telling nobody.

**Build the table before launch**, because a trigger added afterward has no history to fire against.

| Signal | Review trigger | Owner and action | Scheduled checkpoint |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Output quality**, from the eval score | Crosses a threshold drawn from the eval suite, **or shows a sustained directional drift that never crosses it** | Quality owner diagnoses whether the cause is prompt, data or model drift, then decides iterate against re-architect | A periodic output audit against the documentation standard, on schedule, regardless of score |
| **Latency p95** | Crosses the budget set from the user-experience requirement | Investigate the bottleneck, then escalate to a stakeholder review if the budget itself is the thing that is wrong | Usually none, unless latency is masking a logging or traceability gap |
| **Cost per interaction** | Crosses the envelope agreed at intake | Identify the driver, then bring a tradeoff to the stakeholder if the envelope needs revisiting | Usually none, unless a cost control is part of a regulated operating constraint |
| **Residency or configuration posture** | Scheduled confirmation | Confirm and record the posture; flag any drift immediately | Confirmation on the established schedule |

Two rows in that table carry the weight.

**The drift clause on the quality row.** A threshold catches a step change. It does not catch a slope, and a slope is what quality degradation usually looks like. A trigger written only as a threshold will not fire on the failure this section exists to prevent, so the rule needs a directional test alongside the level test.

⚠ **The scheduled column, which fires on a calendar rather than on a number.** In a regulated deployment some reviews must happen when nothing has gone wrong: a periodic output audit against a documentation standard, a scheduled confirmation that the environment still meets a residency rule. **These are design-time obligations rather than tasks to add later**, and a compliance checkpoint that was never wired to a trigger does not surface until a reviewer comes looking for the record. That is the most expensive place to discover it, and the finding is not that the control failed but that nobody can show it ever ran.

**One expectation breaks more often than any signal in the table, and it is cost.** Production volume routinely runs one to two orders of magnitude above the pilot, so a per-interaction figure that was trivial in a proof of concept becomes a material monthly line at scale. Pre-empt it rather than explaining it: give the stakeholder a consumption forecast at expected production volume, name the spend-control posture that will be used, meaning caching, model tiering and budget alerts, and have the tiering conversation before the first invoice rather than after it. **A cost surprise is rarely a cost problem. It is a communication failure with an invoice attached.**

### The loop that pays for itself

Every time a reviewer edits or rejects an output, that is a labeled example, produced as a by-product of work somebody was doing anyway. It is worth stating as a design requirement rather than a nice-to-have: **the review interface should write to the evaluation set.** A system where corrections are made and discarded is throwing away the cheapest quality improvement available to it, and it is throwing away the one signal that arrives with the correct answer already attached.

### Triage: instance or class

**Triage asks one question first: is this an instance or a class?** Fixing an instance adds a rule for the one case that failed. Fixing a class finds the property those cases share. **An improvement program that only fixes instances accumulates a prompt full of special cases and a system nobody can reason about**, and the accumulation is invisible until someone changes the prompt and every special case regresses at once.

| | Instance fix | Class fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Looks like** | Add an example, add a rule, patch the prompt | Re-chunk a document class, change routing, add a tool, rewrite content |
| **Cost** | Minutes | Days to weeks |
| **Effect** | One case | A population |
| **Risk** | Accumulates; regresses under later changes | Larger blast radius, needs full evaluation |
| **When correct** | The case is genuinely exceptional | Three or more instances share a property |

**Decision rule:** three instances sharing an identifiable property become a class item, and no instance fix ships without its case entering the eval set.

**Prioritize on impact times frequency divided by effort**, with two overrides: anything with a governance, risk management and compliance implication goes first regardless of the arithmetic, and anything blocking a segment entirely goes before anything degrading one partially. The backlog lives in the real tracker with the real work, not in a spreadsheet the quality owner maintains privately.

**Closing the loop is what keeps the signal arriving.** Feedback volume is a function of whether the last piece of feedback visibly changed anything. Users who report a problem and see nothing happen stop reporting, and the system then looks healthy because the channel went quiet. **Silence in a feedback channel is a warning, not an achievement.** The fix costs almost nothing: a monthly note naming what was reported, what changed and what was declined with a reason. Declining with a reason maintains the channel; declining silently closes it.

### Expectations, commitments and what a miss means

**An availability commitment and a quality target are different promises with different remedies.** Availability is the system responding. Quality is the answer being right. Conflating them produces the argument in which the vendor says it was up ninety-nine point nine percent of the time and the client says it was wrong.

Quality commitments require the whole evaluation apparatus: a defined metric, a measurement method, a segment breakdown and an agreed threshold. Which means **you cannot make a quality commitment before you have built an evaluation harness**, and if somebody has already made one on your behalf, that is a problem to surface early rather than discover late.

**Set expectations in measurable terms.** "Highly accurate" is not a commitment. "Correct on ninety-two percent of standard invoices, with everything below the confidence threshold routed to review" is. A commitment you can hold has four components:

1. **The metric**, task-appropriate and named
2. **The population it applies to**, since "ninety-two percent accurate" without a scope is meaningless and "ninety-two percent on standard invoices" is a commitment
3. **The routing rule for the remainder**, since a quality target implies that something happens to the cases that miss it
4. **The consequence of a miss**: more review, a rollback, a re-tuning cycle, a conversation. Agreeing this in advance converts a future crisis into a procedure

Two habits hold the arrangement together once it exists. **Agree a review cadence and hold it**, because feedback that arrives only when something has gone wrong is not a loop. And **manage scope against the original success metric**: extension requests are not automatically bad, but each is tested against the metric everyone agreed, and the metric is re-agreed in the open if it changes.

### ⌂ The architect's lens

**The enterprise question this section does not ask.** What do the delivery route and the internal review team commit to underneath the promise you are making to the business? A commitment above what supports it is unbackable.

**Governance at this decision.**

| Decision here | Governance decision that belongs with it | Artifact and owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Committing an availability figure | Checking it against the route's published commitment and the internal team's capacity | Service level stack, owned by the service owner |
| Defining what a miss means | Agreeing the remedy: service credits, cure period, liability cap | Contract schedule, owned by legal |
| Agreeing a quality threshold | Converting it into an error budget that gates releases | Error budget policy, owned by the platform team |
| Capturing corrections as evaluation data | Lawful basis and retention for an evaluation set built from customer records | Data record, owned by the data protection officer |

**What this costs the organization.** A promise the stack cannot support becomes a financial remedy the moment volumes rise. The forgotten cost is the correction loop itself: labeling infrastructure, storage under a retention policy and an evaluation set of customer data nobody classified.

**The executive translation.** We can commit to this number because our vendors and internal teams commit to more, and here is the credit we pay if we miss.

## 8.9 Incident management and operational support

**Severity must account for non-technical harm**, because the worst incidents here are fully available systems producing confident wrong answers at normal latency. A severity scheme inherited from classic operations rates that as a non-incident.

| Severity | Definition | Example | Response |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | Harm occurred or is occurring: unsafe advice acted on, unauthorized disclosure, regulated obligation missed, discriminatory output in a consequential decision | Assistant disclosed one tenant's data to another | Immediate containment, executive notification, ⚠ regulatory assessment |
| **2** | Systematic wrong output in a consequential process, no confirmed harm yet | Wrong threshold cited across a class of approvals for six days | Contain, quantify exposure, notify affected users, review affected decisions |
| **3** | Degraded quality or availability, contained and detected | Retrieval quality dropped after an index rebuild | Standard remediation within business hours |
| **4** | Isolated defect, no pattern | One malformed output | Backlog item |

**The severity-1 category includes harms with no technical signature.** Discriminatory output, unsafe guidance, a missed regulatory deadline caused by wrong information and disclosure through a citation are all severity 1 with every dashboard green. Writing them into the scheme is the only way they get treated as incidents.

### The operational loop

**Notice, triage, reproduce, diagnose, propose, review, capture.**

Notice through monitoring rather than through a user complaint. Triage with the trace and the correlation identifier, which is why the correlation identifier heads the capture set. Reproduce before theorizing. Diagnose against the actual system and the actual data rather than against assumptions about them. Propose a change for human review rather than applying it. **Capture the incident as a regression test**, so the same failure cannot return unnoticed.

### Support is translation, and its measure is whether it reduces future load

The loop above describes the work. This describes the architect's position in it once a team owns the deployment, and the distinction decides whether the architect stays in the loop forever.

**A team reports a symptom. The architect's value is connecting it to an architecture cause.** Latency spiked. Outputs degraded. A tool started failing intermittently. None of those is a cause, and the team pulls in the architect precisely because the mapping from one to the other is the thing they do not yet hold.

**Resolving the incident yourself is firefighting. Teaching the symptom-to-cause path is support**, and the difference is measurable in a way worth stating: firefighting keeps future load constant, and support reduces it. The test is whether the team needs the architect for the new problem or for the familiar one.

The mapping is short enough to be written down, which is what makes it transferable. 8.5's diagnosis table is the full instrument; **this is the subset a first-line engineer can hold**, and it belongs in the team's own runbook rather than in the architect's head.

| Symptom | Likely architecture cause | First action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Quality degraded gradually with no code change** | A model or prompt change, or retrieval drift as the corpus grew | Compare against the eval set; establish what changed in the model, the prompt or the corpus |
| **Latency spiked** | Context size grew, a tool became slow, or the cache stopped hitting | Find the slowest span in the trace: token counts per request, slowest tool call, cache hit rate |
| **Intermittent tool failures** | Authorization, rate limits, or an unhandled error path | Inspect the failing tool's authorization and limits; trace one failed call end to end |
| **Cost rose with no usage change** | Model tier crept up, or caching regressed | Check per-request tier and cache hit rate against the budget model |

**The first row is the one whose absence is expensive**, and its absence has a signature: dashboards stay green for a quarter while answer quality slides, because a gradual decline crosses no threshold. A runbook entry saying that gradual quality decline with no code change points at the model, the prompt or retrieval drift converts that from a quarterly-review discovery into an afternoon's work for a first-line engineer. **The signals were visible throughout. The path from signal to suspect was what nobody had.**

**Two artifacts carry self-sufficiency and they answer different questions.** The **runbook** holds the known symptom-to-cause-to-action paths, so the team resolves what has been seen before. The **escalation path** names who handles what and at which point an issue leaves the team, so people know the boundary of what they are expected to resolve. A team with the first and not the second either escalates everything or nothing.

### The reference design

A scheduled job collects the period's errors. A model reads them, discards noise and deduplicates, so that a hundred instances of one failure are treated as one problem. It diagnoses each distinct issue against the codebase, and it produces a proposed change awaiting human review.

**Note what the design preserves: the machine does the tedium and a human retains the decision.** That is the same disposition as human-in-the-loop design and as the handoff material, and it is the disposition to keep when the volume of operational signal makes automation attractive.

### Agent-assisted diagnosis: what it may touch

The reference design above is a scheduled batch job. The harder case is the live one: an engineer under incident pressure pointing an agent at a production problem. It is the highest-leverage use of the capability and the one most likely to convert an incident into a worse incident, and it resolves into three rules.

**Read before write, enforced by the environment.** Diagnosis is a read activity. An agent doing incident diagnosis should hold read access to logs, traces, metrics, configuration and the repository, with no write access to any of them and with the restriction imposed by the credential and the permission mode rather than by the instruction not to change anything. Plan-mode or an equivalent read-only lock is the correct default for incident work, because the pressure that makes the capability attractive is the same pressure that makes an unreviewed remediation attractive.

**A proposed fix enters normal change control.** The output of agent-assisted diagnosis is a hypothesis and a proposed change, and the proposed change is a change. It goes through the same review, the same approval and the same record as any other, and the fact that it was produced during an incident is a reason to shorten the queue rather than to skip it. An emergency change procedure that already exists is the right route; a new route invented at three in the morning is not.

**The trace identifier is the handoff.** 8.5 names the correlation identifier as the single most important item in the capture set. In diagnosis it is also the interface: the engineer supplies the identifier, the agent reconstructs the run from it, and the reconstruction either succeeds or reveals that the instrumentation is incomplete. An estate where an agent cannot rebuild a failed run from its identifier is an estate where a human cannot either, and the diagnosis exercise has just measured that rather than the incident.

⧉ **The failure mode is confident narrative.** An agent asked why a system failed will produce a coherent causal account whether or not the evidence supports one, and a coherent account arrives during an incident into an audience that wants one. Require the account to cite the specific log lines, trace segments or code paths it rests on, treat an uncited step as a gap rather than as a link and record the diagnosis in the incident record with its evidence so that the post-incident review can test it. A diagnosis that cannot be checked later is a story.

The objective of operational support is not that the architect can operate the system. It is that the team can, without the architect. **Success is the architect's absence being unremarkable.**

### The containment ladder

**Six options, ordered by blast radius. Take the narrowest option that contains the harm.**

| Option | Blast radius | Time to effect | Use when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Disable one tool** | Narrow | Minutes | The harm comes from one capability |
| **Tighten a guardrail or threshold** | Narrow to medium | Minutes | The harm is a class of output, and you accept more false refusals |
| **Route affected traffic to a human** | Medium, and preserves the service | Minutes | The function must continue and quality cannot be trusted |
| **Roll back the prompt** | Medium | Minutes | The regression followed a prompt change |
| **Roll back the model or version** | Wide | Minutes to hours | The regression followed a model change and shadow evaluation was skipped |
| **Kill switch** | Total | Immediate | Severity 1 with ongoing harm and no narrower option contains it |

**Every one of these must be executable without a deployment and tested before launch**, in the readiness gate under the resilience dimension. A kill switch that requires a release is not a kill switch, and a rollback path nobody has exercised is a hypothesis.

**Communication.** Three audiences on three clocks: affected users need to know immediately what to distrust and what to do instead; the business owner needs exposure and expected restoration; the governance, risk management and compliance function needs the facts as facts, early, without speculation about cause. **State what the system got wrong and what people should do about it before you know why**, because the cause takes hours and the exposure continues while you investigate.

**Post-incident review.** Blameless, timeboxed and producing exactly four artifacts: a timeline, a root cause reaching past the proximate trigger, actions with owners and dates and **at least one new eval case**. The last is what makes the review compound rather than repeat. Two questions belong in every such review and are usually missing: how long was this running before anyone noticed, and what would have detected it sooner. Detection latency predicts the severity of the next one.

**⚠ Regulatory notification is a judgment for counsel, not for engineering.** Whether an incident is notifiable, to whom and within what period depends on jurisdiction, sector, the data involved and the nature of the harm, and the clock frequently starts at awareness rather than at confirmation. The operational obligation is to preserve evidence, record the awareness timestamp and escalate to legal and the governance, risk management and compliance function immediately on any severity 1 and on any severity 2 involving personal data, regulated advice or a consequential decision. Do not attempt the notification assessment inside the incident channel.

**⧉ The largest operational risk in this part is undetected quality degradation running in production for weeks.** It has no technical signature, it accumulates consequential wrong decisions the whole time, and the exposure is proportional to detection latency rather than to the size of the defect. Everything in the monitoring and continuous evaluation sections exists to compress that interval, and detection latency is the number to put in front of an executive, because it is the one that converts an abstract quality argument into a quantity of harm.

### ⌂ The architect's lens

**The enterprise question this section does not ask.** What severity is this incident, who is paged out of hours, and does anything about it start a regulatory or contractual notification clock?

**Governance at this decision.**

| Decision here | Governance decision that belongs with it | Artifact and owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Notice, triage, reproduce | Severity classification with a response time and an escalation path per level | Incident severity taxonomy, owned by the service owner |
| Proposing a change for human review | Owning the recurring underlying cause separately from the incident | Problem register, owned by the problem manager |
| Capturing the incident as a regression test | Blameless postmortem producing tracked actions with owners and dates | Action register, owned by the engineering lead |
| Assuming the system is available to diagnose | Degraded mode and recovery time objective when the route is unavailable | Continuity plan, owned by business continuity |

**What this costs the organization.** A loop without severity treats a clinical or financial failure at the pace of a formatting defect, burning the notification window before anyone senior is told. The forgotten cost is the reference design itself: a job reading every error through a model is spend peaking exactly when the system fails.

**The executive translation.** We can tell you inside the notification window which incidents are serious, who is handling them and what the degraded service looks like.

## 8.10 Cost operations and sizing

Cost engineering is choosing the cheap design. **Cost operations is keeping it cheap while other people change it**, a different discipline with different instruments.

### The sizing model

| Input | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| **Volume** | Requests per day, and the **peak rate**, usually several times the average. Peak is what has to fit inside rate limits |
| **Tokens per request** | Split three ways: fresh input at 1x, cache writes at 1.25x and cache reads at 0.1x, with output priced separately and higher. The split is the thing most cost models get wrong. **Count the tokens on the model you will ship**, because the tokenizer changed at 4.7 and later models produce materially more tokens for the same text, so a count carried over from an earlier generation understates the bill by a margin no other line in this table can absorb |
| **Call multiplier** | How many model calls per completed task. Rung 0 on the complexity ladder is a single call, rung 1 is one to a few, rung 7 is a dynamic workflow whose number of calls is variable and composed at runtime, and rung 8, the autonomous agent, is the unbounded one. This is where the ladder and the cost model meet |
| **Unit prices** | Per model, per token type. Perishable; verify |
| **Cost per request** | The arithmetic |
| **Cost per completed outcome** | The number that matters, and the one broken out under unit economics below |
| **Sensitivity** | What happens if conversations get fifty percent longer, retrieved context doubles or volume triples |
| **Feasibility** | Whether it clears the business case at all |

Two refinements the current pricing structure adds. **Cache hits are not deducted against rate limits**, so caching relieves a capacity constraint as well as a cost one. And **the cache hit ratio is the single most informative number in a cost model**, because the gap between 1x and 0.1x is where the money is: a system with a cold cache costs roughly ten times more per input token than the same system with a warm one.
**Two qualifications on the caching and batch lines above, both of which change a cost model rather than refine it.** Caching savings assume the cache is warm when the next request arrives, so a workload whose request frequency is lower than the cache lifetime will not realize them consistently: the model shows a saving the traffic pattern never delivers. And where the batch discount is load-bearing in a regulated deployment, ⚠ verify that batch processing is covered under the applicable business associate agreement and compliance configuration before routing protected data through it, because a cost model resting on a route the compliance position does not cover is not a cost model.


**Three things a sizing model is actually for.**

1. **Killing bad ideas in week one** rather than in month six. This is the most valuable use of it and the one most often skipped.
2. **Choosing between architectures on evidence.** The rungs of the complexity ladder have very different cost profiles, and a sizing model is how you compare them before building either.
3. **Setting expectations you can hold.** Service level commitments need numbers, and these are the numbers.

**The habit worth carrying: refine the prompt on a sample before processing large volumes.** A first-pass success rate of ninety percent against sixty percent across a hundred thousand documents is the difference between a project and an incident, and the sample run costs almost nothing.

### Unit economics

**The unit is a completed task, never a request and never a token.** A system needing two attempts, a retrieval retry and a human correction per success is not cheap whatever its per-call cost. Four figures per use case:

| Figure | Definition | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Cost per attempt** | Total model, retrieval and tool cost for one run | The engineering number |
| **Attempts per completed task** | Including retries and re-asks | The number that turns a cheap call into an expensive outcome |
| **Human minutes per completed task** | Review, correction, escalation handling | Usually the dominant cost and usually unmeasured |
| **Fully loaded cost per completed task** | All three combined | The only figure that belongs in a business case |

**Human minutes decide most business cases and nobody instruments them.** A system that halves model cost and adds two minutes of review per case has made the outcome more expensive, and finance will discover this before architecture does.

### Attribution

Cost must be attributable by team, use case and, where the deployment is shared, by tenant, which requires a cost tag propagated on every call from day one because retrofitting attribution across a shared deployment is close to impossible. **Unattributed cost becomes a central overhead line, and a central overhead line is cut centrally**, usually across all use cases equally, including the ones paying for themselves.

### Accuracy, latency and cost as a trade-off

Nearly everything that improves quality costs time. Agentic systems in particular trade latency and cost for better task performance, and the trade-off is something to decide rather than to inherit.

#### Decomposing the latency budget

"Is a human waiting" decides whether latency is a constraint. It does not tell you where the time goes, and optimizing a system by picking the lever that is easiest to pull is how teams spend a quarter on model latency in a system whose retrieval stage owns most of the wall clock. Allocate the budget across segments before choosing a lever.

| Segment | Typical share of a retrieval-backed request | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Gateway and routing** | Small, and constant | Connection reuse, colocation, removing a hop |
| **Retrieval** | Frequently the largest non-model share | Index choice, candidate count, whether a rerank stage runs, whether the query is expanded |
| **Rerank** | Moderate, and often optional | Reducing the candidate set, a cheaper reranker, or removing the stage where the measured quality gain does not pay for it |
| **Model, time to first token** | Depends on prompt size and cache state | Prompt caching, prefix stability, prompt size |
| **Model, generation** | Proportional to output length | Output trimming, effort, model choice, streaming, which changes perceived latency without changing total |
| **Tool calls** | Unbounded, and the usual surprise | Parallelism where calls are independent, timeouts and removing a call that the design does not need |
| **Post-processing and validation** | Small unless a validation loop retries | Bounding retries, which is where a tail explodes |

**Three rules make the table usable.** Budget against the ninety-fifth percentile, not the median, because the commitment made to users is about the bad case and the median hides it. Instrument every segment separately before optimizing any of them, since 3.9 already requires latency by segment in the trace and this is what it is for. And allocate the whole budget with headroom left unassigned, because a budget allocated to the last millisecond has no room for the retry, the cache miss or the slow dependency that will occur.

⧉ **The tail is the design problem, not the mean.** A system with a good average and an unbounded tail fails in exactly the cases where the user is least tolerant, and the tail is almost always owned by a retry loop, a tool call without a timeout or a cache miss on a cold path. Set an explicit deadline for the whole request, propagate it to every segment so each one knows how much time remains and define what the system returns when the deadline passes. A partial answer delivered on time is a design decision; a complete answer delivered late is often an incident.

**The question that resolves most of these: is a human waiting?**

**Yes.** The path must be real-time and predictable. The available levers:

| Lever | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| **Lower effort** | Trades intelligence for latency and cost within the same model. Frequently the first thing to try |
| **Fast mode** (research preview, Opus 5 and Opus 4.8) | Up to 2.5x higher output **tokens per second** at premium pricing. It does not move time-to-first-token, so it is a lever on the generation segment and not on the wait before the first character. Not available with the batch lane |
| **Prompt caching** | Cuts time-to-first-token; **pre-warming** with `max_tokens: 0` removes the first-request penalty |
| **A smaller model** | Haiku 4.5 for the easy majority, with escalation |
| **Streaming** | Improves perceived latency where total time cannot be reduced |
| **Parallel rather than sequential calls** | Where subtasks are independent |
| **Tighter retrieval** | Less context to process. Reranking reduces cost and latency because the model processes less |
| **Trimming output length** | Output tokens are generated serially, so output length drives total time more than input length |

**No, nothing is blocked.** Batch processing is available at roughly half cost, with a processing window measured in hours rather than seconds and no guarantee on completion time. It suits overnight reports, periodic audits, bulk extraction and back-population. Batch also supports substantially higher output limits on current models via a beta header, which makes it the right lane for very long single outputs regardless of the cost argument.

**The tool-use limitation is narrower than it is usually stated, and getting it wrong excludes batch from workloads it suits.** Server-side tools run normally in a batched request, because the batch worker executes the same agentic loop the synchronous path does and in fact runs more iterations per turn before it pauses. What batch cannot do is a **client-side** tool round trip inside one request, because there is no open connection for your code to return a result on. A paused turn comes back as a result and is continued by submitting a follow-up request. **So the rule is not "no tools in batch". It is that every client-side tool call costs a round trip through the queue**, which is what makes an agent loop with client-executed tools a poor fit for the lane and a server-tool workload a good one.

**The trap:** batch often finishes quickly in practice. That is not a basis for putting it inside a blocking workflow. **A guarantee you do not have is not a guarantee.**

**The planning technique:** work backward from the commitment. If you have promised thirty hours and the lane guarantees twenty-four, submitting every four hours gives headroom. If you have promised two seconds, the lane is unavailable at any price.

**Express the trade-off as a choice with named consequences rather than as a technical constraint.** "Two seconds at this accuracy, or ten seconds at this accuracy, and here is what each error costs" is a decision the business owner can make.

### The optimization playbook, in priority order

One order answers two questions: what to do when a budget alarm fires, and what to do when a system has to be cheaper or faster by design. **The sequence is fixed and it starts with measurement, not with the model.**

1. **Measure.** Find out where the money and the milliseconds actually went, segmented by use case, task class and cohort. It is frequently not where you assumed, and concentration is routinely in a small population doing something nobody designed for
2. **Fix the retry and re-ask loops.** Attempts per completed task is usually the largest multiplier, and it is a quality problem wearing a cost costume
3. **Cache the stable prefix, and restore a collapsed hit ratio.** A collapsed ratio is the most common cause of a cost rise with flat volume, usually a changed prefix rather than a configuration error. Caching cuts latency as well as cost with no loss of content, and pre-warming removes the first-request penalty
4. **Lower effort** where the model supports it. This is often a better lever than switching models
5. **Trim what is not used.** Tool outputs returning forty fields when five matter, retrieved chunks never cited and stale tool results, which **context editing** removes as a platform feature
6. **Defer tool definitions** with tool search, once the catalog reaches roughly ten, or definitions pass 10,000 tokens, or several MCP servers are aggregated
7. **Route by difficulty.** Cheap fast path for the easy majority, escalation for the hard minority. Frequently the largest single saving
8. **Parallelize independent work**
9. **Collapse tool-call chains** with programmatic tool calling, where a sequence could run as one script
10. **Batch what is not blocking**, at roughly half price for work nobody waits on
11. **Stream**, to improve perceived latency where total time cannot be cut
12. **Shorten the output before the prompt**, because output is generated serially. Shorten prompts last, and only with measurement
13. **Only then reconsider the model**, and only with an eval run attached

**Not on the list:** truncating content the task requires, and downsizing the model that does the hard work. Both are common moves and both are wrong.

**Decision rule:** never change the model in response to a cost alarm before measuring attempts per completed task, because a quality problem addressed with a cheaper model becomes a worse quality problem and a larger bill.

### Budget guardrails and hard stops

**Four controls, and the fourth is the one that gets skipped.**

| Control | Mechanism | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Per-request bound** | Maximum tokens, maximum tool calls, maximum turns | Terminate the run, log, degrade gracefully |
| **Per-user or per-tenant quota** | Rolling window | Throttle with an explicit message, never silently |
| **Per-use-case budget alert** | Threshold on the run rate against the monthly budget | Notify the owner, do not stop |
| **Hard stop** | Absolute ceiling per use case | **Stops the use case.** Agreed with the business owner before launch, with a named person who can lift it |

**A hard stop nobody agreed to in advance becomes an emergency negotiation during an incident**, at the worst time with the worst information. Agree the ceiling and the lifting authority at the readiness gate under the commercial dimension. The unbounded agent run is the failure mode this exists for, and it is the one that produces a bill nobody can explain.

### The cost-quality frontier as a decision

Every system sits somewhere on a frontier between cost and quality. **The position should be a decision with a named owner and a date, not a drift.** Systems drift down the frontier through a hundred small optimizations, each individually defensible, none evaluated, until quality has fallen materially and nobody can name the change that did it.

The mechanism that prevents drift is already built: **every cost change goes through the same eval gate as every quality change.** Present the frontier to the business owner as two or three named operating points with measured quality and fully loaded cost per completed task, and let them choose. That is a decision they are qualified to make and it is on the record.

**Decision rule:** a cost reduction that has not been through an eval run is an unmeasured quality change, and it ships under the same gate as any other change or it does not ship.

### ⌂ The architect's lens

**The enterprise question this section does not ask.** What the system costs over three years against the process it replaces, and which budget funds it. Token arithmetic is the first line of the numerator, not the number.

**Governance at this decision.**

| Decision here | Governance decision that belongs with it | Artifact and owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Computing cost per completed outcome | A three year view including reviewer minutes, eval upkeep, support and re-validation | Funded business case over three years. Finance business partner |
| Comparing architectures on cost | Measuring what the incumbent process costs, as the only real comparator | Baseline cost measurement of the current process. Process owner |
| Committing to a volume | Committed spend, capacity allocation and contract term | Commercial agreement with capacity terms. Procurement |
| Running the system past its first year | The condition that would trigger retirement, and the disposition of the index, the traces, the caches and the prompt assets when it is switched off | Service catalog entry with a review date. Service owner |

**What this costs the organization.** Model spend is frequently the smaller bar. Human review on routed exceptions, failed attempts and the amortized cost of owning prompts and the eval program usually dominate, and a case built on token price alone will not survive its first year of actuals. The cost people forget is exit cost, which never appears in the model that justified entering, and which is where the index, the traces, the caches and the prompt assets all finally have to be accounted for.

**The executive translation.** Here is the fully loaded cost per completed outcome against what the current process costs, with a sensitivity for the exception rate doubling.

## 8.11 Documentation and handoff

### The adequacy test

**Can a competent person who has never met you operate this system, diagnose it and change it safely?** If not, the documentation is incomplete regardless of length. It is the only test that matters and it is worth applying literally: name a specific person and ask whether they could.

### The document set

| Artifact | The question it answers | Who reads it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Architecture decision records** | Why is it like this? | Whoever wants to change it |
| **System diagram** | What are the parts? | Everyone |
| **Data flow** | Where does the data go? | Security, legal, compliance |
| **Interface contracts** | What can I rely on? | Integrators |
| **Prompt and evaluation inventory**, versioned | Which prompt produced this, and how do I know if a change helped? | Whoever maintains quality |
| **Runbook** | It broke; what do I do? | Operations |
| **Known limitations** | What does this not do? | Everyone, and it protects you |
| **Escalation matrix and named ownership** | Who decides? | Everyone |
| **System description**, written for external readers | What is this system and what does it do? | External parties: a regulator, an auditor, a customer's procurement function, an affected individual |

The first eight are inward facing and answer three questions: how to operate the system, how to diagnose it and how to change it. The ninth faces outward and is the recurring deliverable most document sets omit, which is why it is treated separately below.

Five of the first eight carry more than a one-line description can show. **Architecture decision records** hold, per significant decision, what was decided, what alternatives were considered, why, what consequences were accepted. **The data flow matters more than the system diagram for review**, because security and legal read the data flow. **Interface contracts** state what goes in, what comes out and what the guarantees are. **The prompt and evaluation inventory** carries versions and locations. **The runbook** covers the common failures, how they present, what to do about each, what to escalate and to whom.

**The decision records are the load-bearing artifact**, because they are the only one that prevents the next person from unknowingly undoing a deliberate choice. Documentation that records what was built but not why is the most common form of inadequate documentation: it describes the system without preserving the reasoning, which means the reasoning is lost the moment you leave.

### The external system description

**Internal documentation and an external description are different artifacts.** They have different audiences, different levels of detail and, most consequentially, different risks. Internal documentation exists so that a competent stranger can operate, diagnose and change the system, and the failure mode of a bad one is an operational failure inside the organization. An external description exists so that a party outside the organization can understand what the system is, what it does to them and what recourse they have, and the failure mode of a bad one is a written representation the organization then has to defend.

**The common failure is sending internal documentation outside.** It happens under time pressure, usually when a procurement questionnaire, a regulator's information request or an individual's query arrives with a short deadline and the only written material in existence is the architecture pack. Internal documentation fails in that use in one of two directions. It either **says too much**, disclosing control placements, thresholds, known weaknesses and vendor arrangements to a reader who did not ask for them and now holds them permanently. Or it **says something the organization cannot stand behind**, because prose written to inform colleagues carries confident claims that were never tested to the standard a representation to an outside party requires.

**What the description contains.** Seven elements, and each is a place the artifact usually goes wrong.

- **Purpose and scope, with explicit exclusions.** What the system is for and what it is not used for. The exclusions do more work than the inclusions, because the reader's question is usually about a use the organization never intended
- **The categories of data used and their sources.** Categories rather than field lists, with the source of each and whether any of it came from the reader
- **The role of the model and what it does not decide.** The most misread point in the artifact. State which determinations the system makes, which it proposes for a person to make and which it has no part in at all
- **The human oversight in place.** What is reviewed, by whom, on what basis and what happens when a reviewer disagrees. A bare statement that outputs are reviewed, with no description of the review, is the claim most likely to be tested
- **Known limitations and error characteristics, stated honestly.** Where the system performs worse, what it is known to get wrong and roughly how often. A description with no limitations is read as either incomplete or untrue, and both readings cost more than the disclosure would have
- **The review and escalation route available to someone affected.** How a person raises a concern, who receives it, what happens next and within what period. A named route, not an invitation to contact the organization
- **The version and the date.** Because the description will be produced again years later against a system that has changed

**Every claim in it must be one the evidence register can support.** This is the discipline that governs the whole artifact. The description is the document that will be read back to the organization, by a regulator during an inquiry, by a customer during a dispute, by counsel during litigation. A claim with no artifact behind it is an unbacked representation, and the moment to discover that is while writing rather than while answering. Work the draft against the register developed in 4.9 sentence by sentence: name the artifact that evidences each claim, and delete or soften every claim that has none. Descriptions written the other way round, drafted first and evidenced later, are how an organization ends up defending a sentence nobody can source.

**It is a governed artifact rather than a marketing page.** It has a named owner, a version history and a review cadence tied to material change in the system, and it clears the same approval as any other external representation. A description drafted once by whoever was available and then reused for two years describes a system that no longer exists, and the gap is discovered by the reader rather than by the organization. The transparency element developed in 4.5 sets what has to be disclosed and to whom; this is the artifact that discharges it.

⚠ Whether a description of this kind is required at all, what it must contain and to whom it must be given are set by the regime the deployment sits under and by the contracts in force, and that determination is counsel's rather than an architectural default.

**The two audiences read it differently.** A regulator reads for what is missing and a customer reads for what is promised, and a description that satisfies one and not the other is not finished.

### The outcome document, which is a third audience again

The inward-facing set answers how to operate, diagnose and change the system. The external description answers what the system is, for a regulator or a customer. **Neither answers the question the person who funded the work will ask, which is what the deployment produced.** That takes a third artifact, written for a sponsor who was not on the build and has to justify the deployment upward.

The failure it prevents is specific and it is easy to walk into. An architect closes an engagement and writes the outcome document from the metrics easiest to export: request volume, average latency, error rate. The sponsor takes it to a finance audience, who asks what the deployment saved or produced, and the document cannot answer. **Volume, latency and error rate establish that the system runs. None of them is a business outcome**, and a document that is complete as a technical record can be useless as a case for expansion.

**Six fields, and the last three are the ones that get left out.**

| Field | What it records |
| --- | --- |
| **Use case with scope boundary** | What the deployment does, and explicitly what it does not |
| **Metric before** | The business metric as it stood before deployment, in the unit the business already tracks |
| **Metric after** | The same metric, measured on the same definition. A changed definition between the two is not a comparison |
| **Control in place** | What makes the before-and-after auditable rather than asserted |
| **Measurement owner** | Who owns ongoing measurement once the engagement closes |
| **Reuse potential** | How the pattern transfers to other engagements |

**The before metric has to be captured at the start, which is the operational consequence of this whole section.** It cannot be reconstructed afterward, and its absence is unrecoverable: without it there is no story, and with it but without a control the after number is an assertion. This is the same discipline as the pre-build baseline in 1.2 and the value statement in 8.7, arriving at the other end of the lifecycle. **The value statement argues that the system is worth building. The outcome document establishes what it turned out to be worth**, and the two are only comparable because they use the same metric and the same definition.

⧉ **The measurement owner field is the one that decides whether the document stays true.** Every other field is a snapshot. That one names who keeps measuring after the person who wrote it has gone, and a document with no measurement owner has an expiry date nobody has been told about.

### The framing for people who see documentation as overhead

Documentation is the mechanism by which a design survives the departure of its author. A system nobody dares change is a system that will be replaced rather than maintained, and replacement is more expensive than documentation by orders of magnitude.

### ⌂ The architect's lens

**The enterprise question this section does not ask.** Where do these artifacts live, who owns them once the architect has moved on, what detects that the diagram no longer matches the running system, and what does the organization hold that proves it can operate the system without the people who built it?

**Governance at this decision.**

| Decision here | Governance decision that belongs with it | Artifact and owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Producing the document set | Placing it in a governed repository with versioning and a review cadence | Repository entry, owned by the architecture function |
| Writing a data flow for security and legal | Assigning it to information governance rather than to the build team | Data view, owned by the information governance lead |
| Applying the adequacy test once | Detecting drift, with a review date and a named reviewer | Review schedule, owned by the service owner |
| Documenting design decisions | Producing the intended-use statement where a regime treats documentation as a deliverable | Documentation set, owned by compliance |
| Declaring the handoff complete | Assembling the operating model, the rota, the entitlement register and cost attribution as evidence of readiness | Operational readiness pack, owned by the service owner |
| Treating handoff as knowledge transfer | Baselining the delivery and incident metrics that will show whether it worked | Metrics baseline, owned by the engineering lead |

**What this costs the organization.** Documentation without an owner outside the delivery team decays at the rate the system changes, and the failure surfaces as an audit finding rather than as an outage. Handoff declared complete on a training attendance count rather than on evidence leaves the run team holding a system it cannot diagnose, which appears as escalation volume for two quarters and as slower resolution against a commitment somebody has signed. Two costs are forgotten: the recurring review effort, which is a standing allocation on someone's objectives rather than a one-time write, and the builders, who remain the real support function while nominally working on the next thing.

**The executive translation.** This document set earns its cost only once it has an owner outside the build team and a scheduled review date, and the handoff is finished when the readiness evidence exists and escalations back to the build team are measurably falling, not when the training has been delivered.

## Operations and Measurement: the one-page version

1. Readiness has eight dimensions, binary evidenced conditions, three outcomes and named signatories, and **a gate nobody can fail is not a gate.** Where several conditions are open at once, measurement and ownership are the absences that matter most, because they prevent you fixing the rest.
2. Write the eval suite before the production code. It forces a measurable definition of success, exposes design assumptions while changing them is cheap, and gives you a gate with a pre-change baseline.
3. Evaluation is the asset that outlives any prompt. Make the success criterion specific, measurable, achievable and relevant; measure the five families of accuracy, latency, cost, safety and security; combine a code grader for validity with a model grader for quality; have the grader reason and then discard the reasoning.
4. Prioritize volume over quality by automating the grading rather than keeping the set small, reserve humans for calibration and sampled review, and freeze the dataset so comparison keeps meaning something.
5. **A stale eval suite is worse than none**, because it passes while measuring behavior the system no longer produces. Update the set in the same change as the behavior it measures.
6. The evaluation harness is the component most often specified and least often built, so ask to see it running: thirty to fifty cases, two prompt versions, segment reporting and a deliberate breakage. Every run emits a manifest pinning model, sampling settings, dataset, grader, index and code version, because a score without one cannot be reproduced or defended. A number that moves when a known defect is fixed is what makes the harness an instrument.
7. Multi-step and multi-turn are different categories. Score a multi-step run on outcome as primary and on trajectory against constraints rather than against a reference path, charge the first step whose output was wrong rather than a fraction of steps completed, and separate the three tool-call failures that share one symptom. Multi-turn needs its own golden dataset of full transcripts and catches what single-turn scoring cannot see.
8. Quality is a service level indicator with a measurement lag, so instrument fast proxies and shrink the exposure window. Commit to availability, latency percentiles and a measured quality level on a named population, never to correctness on a case.
9. You cannot commit to availability you do not control, so take one of three positions and disclose which: pass-through, degraded mode or multi-provider. **An unevaluated fallback trades a visible outage for an invisible quality event.** Write the quality objective with a population, an instrument, a window and an action on a miss, run an error budget against it, and when the number drops localize in a fixed order beginning with the harness.
10. Monitoring has six layers, and stopping at three reports a healthy system producing wrong answers. Alert only where a response is defined. Capture the correlation identifier, the prompt and model version and the three token fields, or the trace answers nothing.
11. Logs tell you the system ran and only evaluation tells you it was right. Watch five drifts, and remember user drift is the one always missed.
12. Absence of errors is not evidence of health, so sample the high-confidence stratum and alert on distribution shift.
13. Classify the failure before attributing it: prompt failure, hallucination, model mismatch or an orchestrator-workers boundary. **Stronger instruction never fixes a hallucination.**
14. Evaluation becomes a running control with six instruments. The golden set grows by addition, comparison runs offline before online, the judge is calibrated on a schedule, and all five change types are gated including corpus publication, which is the one omitted everywhere.
15. Decide the sample size, the primary metric and the stopping rule before the test. Where exposure to a worse version is unacceptable, shadow testing is the design rather than the fallback, and its cost is the loss of downstream signal.
16. Metrics are four levels on four clocks. Refuse the vanity metrics because each rises as the system worsens, name the attribution method rather than letting the reader assume a stronger one, and measure the baseline before launch or agree value will not be claimed. The value statement answers the earlier question of whether to build at all: a baseline in a business unit, the post-deployment state in the same unit, the run cost taken from the sizing model and a payback period quoted with its sensitivity.
17. The improvement loop needs a cadence, an owner and a queue. It triages instance against class, writes every correction back into the eval set, and closes visibly or the signal stops.
18. Build the governance table before launch, mapping each signal to a trigger, an owner and an action, including the drifts that never cross a threshold and the regulated checkpoints that fire on a calendar.
19. An availability commitment and a quality target are different promises, and a quality commitment needs a metric, a population, a routing rule and an agreed consequence for a miss.
20. Incident severity must include harm with no technical signature. Run the loop from notice to capture, let the machine do the tedium while a human keeps the decision, and contain with the narrowest of six options, all executable without a deployment. ⚠ Notifiability is counsel's judgment.
21. Support is translation, not firefighting. Leave the team a runbook of symptom-to-cause paths and an escalation boundary, so you are needed for the new problem rather than the familiar one.
22. Cost operations sizes on volume, token split, call multiplier and cache hit ratio, tracks fully loaded cost per completed task including human minutes, attributes it from day one, fixes retries before touching the model, and treats the cost-quality frontier as a decision rather than a drift. Decompose the latency budget by segment before choosing a lever and budget against the ninety-fifth percentile, because **the tail is the design problem, not the mean**, and it is owned by a retry loop, an untimed tool call or a cold cache.
23. Documentation passes one test: whether a competent stranger could operate, diagnose and change the system. The decision records are load-bearing because they preserve the reasoning rather than the shape.
24. The ninth artifact faces outward, a system description written for a regulator, an auditor, a procurement questionnaire or an affected person, every claim in which the evidence register has to support, because sending internal documentation outside either says too much or says something the organization cannot stand behind.
25. A tenth artifact faces the sponsor: the outcome document, carrying the before metric, the after metric on the same definition, the control that makes the comparison auditable and the measurement owner. **The before metric cannot be reconstructed later.**
26. The handoff is complete when the evidence exists and escalations back to the build team are falling, not when the training has been delivered.
